Sr. A. Serafina will join the community as vice-superior and alms-collector; she commends her to her. She writes nothing about the house, since she is about to go to Rome; on her return she will visit her.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Good Superior

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. The Delegate of S. P. d'Arena will send you Sr. A. Serafina; present her to the sisters as Vice-Delegate; she will take Sr. A. Ermelinda with her when she goes collecting alms.1 Never change her; for now she will account only to me for the money she receives; never ask her for any of it, except a little in extreme need.

  2. She will bring her camp bed, mattress, pillow and blanket; if you could put her in your room, at the foot of your bed, I would be pleased, if there is room.2

  3. You will have received my letter announcing my departure for Rome, so it is pointless to discuss everything now. On my return I shall come there and everything will be arranged; meanwhile ask around whether you could have a small flat from some benefactress.3

  4. I do [not] stop writing and appealing to my friends, and let us hope God will move some good heart for us; then I will write a letter to Sr. A. Serafina for the Marchioness Santi,4 and let us hope she will do something, as she has already shown she can.

5. Goodbye; everything you have done is fine; wait a few more days before calling the doctor; rub her with oil and camomile and then wrap her in the cloth, making sure it has been heated in the frying pan.5 Make a novena to the Eternal Father, trust in him, and she will be healed.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you; I am your

Mother Rosa G.

P.S. Never send Sr. A. Serafina to sit up at night; you may only send her on checking visits,6 never to nursing, because she suffers and falls ill.

She tells her to open the letters addressed to her and send on only those she must answer personally. If the printer has printed the prayers composed by the Father, she should send some. For running the house and accepting girls and postulants, she should pray and then act as she thinks best.1

[Our daughter]

  1. A line to tell you two small things: first, you must open and read all letters addressed to the house and then lock them away, because in the one you sent me you enclosed a certificate: it was Count Gazzola recommending Maddalena; those you see need an answer from me, send them on.2

  2. Now see whether the printer has got ready a few of the prayers the Father wrote; send them at once.

  3. As for the little girl you mention, do whatever you think right; take whom you like, and the same for the postulants; pray, and then go ahead, and God will be with you.

  4. Write to Sr. A. Serafina to keep the letter and take it herself when the lady returns from the country; and tell Maria that the Father is in Rome.3 I can't understand Fr. Luigi; I have seen nothing yet.

I am your poor

Mother Rosa

She has been in Rome five days but has done and obtained nothing. Much prayer is needed to move the hearts of good people to help the Work of Saint Anne. Only Jesus can do it. She addresses a fervent prayer to him for the Daughters of Saint Anne, true Daughters of the Eternal Father. She always keeps them in mind and commends them to God.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I received your letter telling me about Sr. A. Fortunata and the Parish Priest.1 Let us bless the Lord, who knows so well how to beautify the poor deeds of the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.

  2. My daughter, this is already the fifth day I have been in this holy City and I have done nothing yet, obtained nothing.2 Let us pray; yes, pray fervently to the heart of Jesus to move the hearts of good people to help the work of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.

  3. Only he can, because he must work for this Work of his Grandmother, since it belongs to his Eternal Father.3 My Jesus, what should matter more to you than this Work, if not that your Father be glorified? These poor creatures, the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, have him constantly on their lips and call on him in all their actions; they hold him in their heart because they love him as Father, placing all their good in him; they adore him in his most exalted

dignity and learn every delight in his divinity; in short, you can well say: «They are the true Daughters of my Eternal Father, for they expect everything from him and rest in him alone».4 My Jesus, is this not true? And can your heart be slow to help these creatures in what they need, and especially the one most in need of all, his slave?

  1. What am I saying, my God! The moment I am in is so important — what a great worry fills my mind. Patience! God be blessed in all things.

  2. Pray, pray, press the dear Heart hard. I always keep you in mind wherever I go; I always carry all my blessed daughters with me, and especially the Superiors, whom I commend to God every day that he may give them light to direct their communities well.5

Goodbye, I am your Poor

Mother [Rosa Gattorno]

God bless you all, and one day may the God who was so favourable to you here on earth be merciful to you in heaven.6

If prayer does not miraculously obtain what we want, the horizon looks dark, but the Father's right hand can scatter everything, and the Daughters of Saint Anne will be able to carry the light of faith to the whole world. She longs to return within the walls of Saint Anne's house. She asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I hope you have received all our letters. My blessed daughter, if prayer does not miraculously obtain what we want, this horizon looks very dark for us;1 but the right hand of our Eternal Father can scatter everything in an instant, and the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, may enjoy the most beautiful light in all Catholicism and make it shine in the most idolatrous lands and plant there the standard of Saint Anne.2

  2. I am glad to hear the good news you give me of the little girls; I bless God for it, asking him to continue pouring on them the dew of his mercies; pray and have others pray.

  3. I am fairly well, only I find myself away from our centre.3 What a different way of living! I always feel I must go and see — what? The dear walls of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate. A hole, even the smallest and narrowest, but in your house, my dear Mother.4

■Hfl

  1. Goodbye; the Lord bless you, and may his gifts be so abundant that they console and sanctify you. And the same for all the others; please read them this line.

  2. Our dear Daughters, pray and storm the heart of Jesus so that this poor Mother of yours may soon obtain everything; so far I have done nothing; how painful it is for me to be outside the walls of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate! Pray, for these are very sad times.

Goodbye; the Lord pour out on you his choicest blessings. I am your

Poor and affectionate Mother Rosa

She has learned from her letter the amount of the debt and is greatly worried. She will leave Rome in five days. A French Religious will arrive in Piacenza; she is to welcome her with every courtesy and tell her of the Mother's imminent return.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter,

  1. I received your last letter, in which I found the figures of everything you owe.1 What can we do? Pray, pray; and as for me, God alone knows the pain and anguish I feel; last night when it reached me it was late, and I assure you it gave me no more rest, with the miller always before me.2 What pain, what sorrow, my God!

  2. Here I have been able to get nothing, or practically nothing, for it is very little; alms are no longer to be found.

  3. Now, God willing, we finally leave Rome on Wednesday evening at 9, and I cannot fix the time of our arrival because I must stop in Bologna, but I will telegraph you on the way or from Bologna.3

  4. Listen, on Wednesday a Religious is to come who is not dressed as a Religious; she is French.4 As soon as you receive this, tell the portress to let her in the moment she arrives and say nothing about whether we are in or not; let her call you, and you will tell her at once: I have received letters from the Mother saying Your Reverence was to come, and since the Mother could not leave Rome until Wednesday, she wrote to me to keep you here until

she arrives. The Mother hopes to be here on Friday morning at the latest.5

  1. Show her every kindness, and for sleeping I would like you to put her in the Teacher's room, asking the Teacher to move wherever you think best, even for the moment into the room where the nurses have their lessons;6 and let the guest room be thoroughly clean. I hope you have had the piano taken away, as it was useless.

  2. So this Religious will stay with you in the Teacher's room; see that she does not leave. If you can't understand her, call Sr. A. Angiola;7 have prayers said that I may arrive alive and that the return journey may not be as painful as the journey here, for I really did not think I would make it.8

I am your most affectionate M. R. God bless you and all the others.

7. Greet everyone for me, and the Delegate9 in particular; tell her I am not writing to her because there is no point, we shall see each other soon.

She tells him simply that the author of the Rule is Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, to whom she turned after a vision. She begs that the Father be allowed to act freely in the Institute.1

Most Holy Father,

  1. For fifteen years, at God's command, I have increased my bodily austerities with the most agonising penances; my food is herbs or pulses; most of these penances are for the Church; Jesus taught me all the instruments he wanted me to use. Now I am most cruelly distressed by a strong fear that they will take my life, or that I shall no longer be able to work in the Lord's work; I am seized by violent attacks that bring me to the point of death; the last time, God commanded me to write to Your Holiness, and I would find relief.

  2. The Rule I presented to Your Holiness was not written by me; while I was praying in the Chapel, Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, appeared to me, and the Servant of God Father Bernardo Maria Clausi told me to go to Mr. Tornatore, Missionary, who would give me the book of our Constitutions. Three times I resisted obeying this command, but the third time I was threatened, and then I obeyed. He is therefore our Founder; he has been working for five years; now the houses are increasing and I, weakened, can barely stand.

  3. I would need a line from Your Holiness so that this Missionary, without diminishing his vocation in the least, could act freely in this work.2

Most Holy Father, deeply prostrate at your most holy Feet, I implore the longed-for grace.

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

If Providence does not come, it is because Jesus likes to be asked. The month of June favours meditation and contemplation of the Sacred Heart.1

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

  1. I hear Providence is making you sigh; do you know why? It wants us to pray more and more, and our dear Jesus likes to be asked.2

  2. Daughter, what a beautiful month! There is no need even to read the point for meditation, with the Heart of Jesus open. There, there, my dear, take your mind and heart; there you will find everything and rest sweetly.

Goodbye, the Lord bless you all; I am your

P. M. Rosa

She asks him to intercede with the Holy Father to reply to a note of hers.1

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I beg Your Most Reverend Eminence to have the charity to set my mind at rest about my fear of not obtaining from His Holiness what I desire.2 Your Eminence alone can obtain everything for me in answer to the little note I handed His Holiness.3

  2. I ask Your Most Reverend Eminence to hear one who, deeply humbled at your feet, awaits the Apostolic Blessing, as she signs herself with the greatest veneration

Your Most Reverend Eminence's most humble, most obedient Servant Sr. Anna

Maria Rosa Gattorno

She encloses a letter for the Princess and asks her to deliver it. They have received the Holy Father's blessing and she will be able to bring her a Crucifix he has blessed. Courage; the Lord will soon console her.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter,

  1. I have just received two lines from you, forwarded from Piacenza with Sr. A. Serafina's. I enclose a letter for Maria, the Princess.2 Send it at once to Sr. A. Serafina.

  2. Courage; the Holy Father blessed us, and you will also have a crucifix blessed by the Holy Father.3

  3. Pray. Goodbye. I am glad to hear the Sister is better. Blessed be God, who knows how to do everything for our good. Yes, my blessed daughter, you will see that the Lord will soon console you.

  4. Meanwhile, for vegetables and potatoes, tell Sr. A. Serafina to go and get them from the gardener at S. P. d'Arena, and I will see to it afterwards; indeed you can have as many potatoes fetched as you like. God bless you.

In haste, your poor

Mother Rosa

She should have much prayer offered to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and seek strength and consolation in him, and she will be heard. She should urge one Sister to be prudent in speech and point out to another her fault against the Rule.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter, wholly ours

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. A few hours ago I received your last letter, dated the 3rd, and I also received all the others you mention in it.2

  2. My dear, have much prayer offered to this dear Heart of Jesus — what a sweet month! — the Heart of Jesus that receives our every poor sigh; so, my beloved, take everything to this heart, go and get everything from this heart, and you will find everything. Say to him: «Dear Jesus, let me too taste just one little drop of your sweetest nectar», and you will see that Jesus will give you everything, because he wants to hear us seek it and to give it to those who truly long for it with faith and openness.3 God gives this to the simple and not to the wise of this world.4

  3. Everything you write me is fine; I am delighted with what you tell me about the Heart of Jesus, and I bless God.

  4. Silence, for charity's sake; impose silence on Sister Sr. A. Felicita — silence.5 You are also right about Sr. A. del Buon Pastore, who did not do well; call her and tell her: «My daughter,

listen, without realising it you broke a rule, because you should not have revealed to your sister what you had received in church, but should have come only to me. So from now on please do not do it again», and then you will hear what she says. You will answer: «The Mother and the Father will soon come, and you can tell them everything».6

Goodbye, my dear; the Lord bless you and all the others; I am your

Affectionate Mother Rosa

She shares in her sufferings. She should try to obtain free baths for the girl with scrofula. She answers her questions, advising how to act. She should make a novena to St Joseph.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday I received your letter and hear of all your troubles; at once I asked the Lord to transfer them onto my shoulders, for my chest already shares the pain.1

  2. My God, how cruel the news of the poor little girl was to me!2 Patience; you should get the Doctor to write a certificate showing that she needs baths, and then go to Monsignor's Chaplain to see whether he can get her sent to the baths, as Count Caracciolo did; and the certificate should say she has scrofula; but do it at once.

  3. For taking the boys to confession you can send two religious, but [accompanied] by the Teacher; choose those who seem most capable to you.3

  4. As for work, I have just received letters from the Delegate of S. P. d'Arena, who is sending some, and then the Delegate of the Dal Verme House can give you some.4

  5. As for adoration, do what you can; God is content at once when we do what we can; so let us do everything with holy simplicity, love God the Father very much and try

to obtain everything from him. He is all patience and meekness, all Charity and love; and our holy Mother Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, was adorned with these virtues.5

  1. Make a novena to St Joseph and say to him: hear us, dear support of the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate; and you will see that providence will come; but don't bully the saints; pray to them with patience and resignation.6

  2. Goodbye, my dear daughter; the Lord bless you and make you holy. Greet them all for me and tell them I wish them the choicest blessings from Heaven that a creature can share.

Goodbye; I am your Poor Mother Rosa

She should give precise information about Sr. A. Ernesta. Courage: trials are needed to progress in holiness. From meditation on the poverty of Bethlehem and Nazareth she will draw «every delight».

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have [just] received another letter from you, and one yesterday, telling me about Sister Sr. A. Ernesta. I cannot make out which one she is: the cook or the other one who arrived with Sr. A. Santina's sister?1 When you answer, please tell me clearly who she is, so that I can understand.

  2. I also hear about this one's unease; try to see where all her bad behaviour comes from, and then we will think about it.2 As for the other matter you mention, be patient; everything will be settled. I will come very soon; for now I am too busy here and cannot move, but I do not stop writing and thinking to get a little corner for you.3

  3. Do you see that the moment of suffering I spoke of has come? But would it not have been to be feared that it was not the Lord's will for these Religious to live in Genoa?4 So courage, for the moment of trial is necessary; courage and patience, peace, resignation; with these everything is obtained and every obstacle overcome.5

  4. What shall I say to the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate? Only that in time of trial great strides are made on the way of holiness, and our soul is adorned with virtues and grows great, and finally, when peace returns, enjoys its fruit, sharing in the delights of its beloved Jesus.

  5. Courage: your tribulations are few compared with the house of Nazareth, which lacked everything, and in it lived the three richest personages of Heaven; there was no bed, only straw, in the Hut at Bethlehem, and yet the Son of God chose it as his first dwelling and willed to be born there; the Queen of Heaven and earth seated where? On straw, beside a manger, feeding only on the beautiful light of Jesus. In him she found everything: the comforts and delights of the world; everything was contained in that dear Child.6

  6. And you, who can look at him within your heart, will find every delight if you keep your gaze on him alone. Blessed be God always, who deigns to lower his most holy hand.

Goodbye; be ever the blessed ones in your tribulations.7 I am

Your Poor Mother Rosa

She suggests how to deal with a difficult sister.1 She is eager to return soon among her daughters;2 it is hard to live outside the walls of the religious house, but she is also convinced that eternal life in Paradise must be earned. There are the first four sisters, who form Saint Anne's retinue.10 She is consoled and strengthened by the thought that none of her daughters will die without obtaining salvation.

I hear that Signora Caterina gave you F 30. Poor dear, she is clearly always thinking of you.6

  1. Daughters, pray that I may soon be done,7 for these days, I assure you, I am in the greatest distress, and everything is getting so complicated that only prayer can open the way and free us from so many anxieties.

  2. My little brain works night and day, and the anxiety I feel is very strong, seeing myself in someone else's house, and thinking of you, and seeing myself held captive — and who knows for how much longer!

  3. Oh, my daughters, believe me, many times Sr. A. Vincenza and I do long for a little corner in our own house, together with our Sisters, for here everyone watches us,8 and so often we have to bear great hardship because we cannot even have water.3 Do you see, my dears, what it costs to be outside our walls?4

  4. Ah, daughters, believe me, we do not reach paradise unless we have first earned eternal life with toil.5 Up there everything is over.6 The Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, will have an eminent place near the Mother of the Immaculate, as the four who had the good fortune to enter into rest there already form her retinue.10

  5. None will die without being saved and being sure of Paradise, with little Purgatory. This thought alone, believe me, is enough to give me strength and courage to face any torment whatever, any persecution, because everything fades before this most beautiful horizon.711 What is a torment caused by men compared with the lovely caresses Jesus will give us?

I close because it is very late and my health is poor, as usual.

God bless you and make you happy. Goodbye; I am your

poor Mother S. A. M. Rosa

  • Sr. A. Daria Vagni, died at Cento on 22.8.1867;

  • Sr. A. Blandina Grossi, died at Sampierdarena on 15.2.1870;

  • Sr. A. Crocifissa Dugoni, died at Sampierdarena on 30.7.1870;

  • Sr. A. Benedetta Stabelini, died at Piacenza on 6.11.1870.

8 We are under everyone's eyes.

9 The reasons for discomfort are many, but in every painful situation she finds the gospel side: the Kingdom of heaven suffers violence (Mt 11:12).

She reports on the purpose and state of the Institute as regards the Religious, those assisted and the houses. She asks for its approval.1

Most Holy Father,

  1. The undersigned Petitioner, prostrate at the most holy feet of Your Beatitude, humbly sets forth that she is at the head of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate Virgin and Mother of God, founded five years ago.2

  2. The purpose of the said Institute is to honour the Saint's privilege of being Mother of the Immaculate.

  3. Its primary works for the neighbour are home nursing of the sick of both sexes, by day and by night, and taking in girls at risk to safeguard their innocence.

  4. With the permission of the respective Ordinaries four houses have been founded: two in Piacenza, the third in S. P. D'Arena and the fourth in Genoa.

  5. The Religious number about 80; the girls at risk they have taken in number about 120, all so far relying on Divine Providence.3

  6. The Petitioner humbly asks a special blessing on herself and her Religious, and a word of approval from You, so as to be sure that the Institute is a plant of the heavenly Father and to be encouraged to continue the work.

  7. To present her petition, the Petitioner takes the occasion of the solemn privilege the Immaculate grants to Your Holiness's Pontificate, namely that of completing its twenty-fifth year.

Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

Suggestions on some situations reported in the letters she is answering. In Rome the Institute's affairs have become complicated. She should pray asking the intercession of St Francis of Paola.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My blessed daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received your very long letter yesterday. You make me laugh by asking me about certain little things you ought to do yourself. How good it would have been if you had sent the linen the Bishop's Chaplain was asking for with a little note of apology!1 I wrote to the Delegate of the Morte to go there about the little girl;2 if she has not yet gone, you can go together and offer the apologies charity teaches us.

  2. In your other letter you told me you were left alone with the girls' Teacher.3 For charity's sake, don't trust him, for Cepinetto is cunning and schemes everything to catch us in his nets.

  3. You also said you would tell me something about Sr. A. Gioacchina, what Sr. A. Giovanna was saying.

  4. You tell me you spent the money you received differently. Very well; let us hope the Lord sends you enough to pay the miller too.4 My dear, if the Lord grants us to pay them all, write and tell me, for I assure you it will be a consolation amid so many fierce tribulations that give me no more rest.

  5. Pray, for charity's sake, for our affairs have become so tangled and everything so bitter that my poor brain can no longer take it in, so great is the crowd of thoughts it holds.5

  6. You did very well to send [someone] to that lady, the Inspector's wife; and what does it matter if she has such an illness? Is she not worthy of being nursed? Indeed I feel special affection and compassion for her, for such people deserve them.6

  7. In one letter you tell me Sr. A. Bernardina is getting fat, and in your last you say she is just the same; that does not prevent the schoolroom being kept tidy even though her bed is there.

  8. As for replying to the letter you sent me from the man in Crema, tell him to send them at once and to bring what little they can, at least the entrance [dowry], or else their papers in order for what little they have.7 You must do this somewhat on your own, and I assure you that when I receive your letters and see that you act as God inspires you, they bring me immense consolation. Courage: it is in battle that we must grow strong.

  9. I would like you to begin the Fridays to St Francis of Paola for me, and Superior Francesca too, so that God may hear me according to my intention. I too will begin them next Friday.8

  1. From what I see, I shall not be able to be there before the end of the month, God willing and if everything is finished. Don't mention these Fridays when you write; it is enough for me to know you received this letter.

  2. You mention the firewood. What can I tell you? My dear, Signora Scopesi said she would send a cartload.9 If you think fit, pay her a visit and meanwhile ask whether she wants anything from Rome, for I fear she may take it badly if we say nothing to her.

Goodbye for now, for I still have to say all my prayers and it is already 6 in the evening.

Goodbye; I am yours for ever, Poor Mother. God bless you all.

Superior Francesca is in extreme poverty. She should try to help her in some way.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My beloved daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received a letter from the Delegate Francesca, and she tells me she is in extreme poverty. See whether you can help her, give her something, and go together to someone; as for getting a place at the baths for the girl, since you are going to the Prefect, you can ask him.1

Nothing more for now. Goodbye, my dear; pray and have others pray. God bless you; I am your

Poor M. Rosa

She is deeply pained to hear that providence is lacking and suggests asking charitable people for help. She describes the conditions of Christians in Rome. The Institute's affairs are dragging on; both she and Fr Tornatore are suffering not a little. She asks for detailed news of the house's debts.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter, wholly mine

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received another letter from you. Yesterday I received the other very long one. How it pains me to hear that providence is failing you! I feel my heart breaking with grief. Why don't you take courage and go to some pious person? The Marchioness Anguissola, for instance; tell the Parish Priest, for charity's sake; don't let yourselves be reduced to despair.1

  2. Now you may think that here we are enjoying feasts and ceremonies of the Holy Father. Daughter, quite the opposite. I can tell you that Rome is pitiful to see: all Christians live as if in prison; no one can shout a «viva» without being put in prison at once. The Holy Father is always imprisoned.2 The delegations that come are booed by ruffians. In short, everything comes down to prayers and penances: processions of women and of men, and prayers in the churches, in silence. One cannot go out, for every moment they stone the Priests; they hold demonstrations against the nuns. The Jews make tremendous uproars, and we are obliged to

stay indoors out of constant fear.3

  1. Then add our affairs, which move so slowly that they cause us immense pain — my God!4 I assure you it is a continual agony. The Father too suffers a great deal, as one can see, and as you will see too; but if we go on at this pace we shall not be able to be there before early July.5 What patience! But let everything be for the greater glory of our Eternal Father; to him everything, and to us the misery of Adam.

  2. If by chance you find yourselves with nothing, turn to Sig. Brigidini to advance you two hundred francs, or in my name, and you can share some of it with the Delegate of the Morte.6

  3. You mention the little girls in the garden: provided they are with you and well supervised, you may take them.

  4. Have you still given nothing to the pharmacist? You ask whether you should give the 400 f. to the miller; you may, but where did you give the F. 600? Have you paid all the small bills? Try, if you can, to give something to the pharmacist; and always send something to those of the Morte.7

  5. How it pained me to hear about the soup. Patience! What can we do? Pray, and I assure you I pray always, and more so here, where we are always alone and I go out8 only on the House's business and nothing else. God's will be done; what suffering, but always gladly, because it is all for Jesus. The Lord bless you all, and you in particular, for whom I invoke him with all my affection. Goodbye; I am your Poor Mother.

Have this letter read to the Delegate of the Morte as well.

I am your Poor M. Rosa

8. P.S. I am not writing because my hands are so swollen that it is too much effort. Believe me, I am in martyrdom. You will hear when I come, and I am sure you will be amazed. If you have not yet written to those for whom I enclose letters here, send these and put the date of Piacenza on them.9 Carlotta not very well.

Her letters have brought consolation. She speaks of the sad situation in Rome, of the Holy Father and of the Religious. No outcome is in sight for the Rule.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received all your letters, and I assure you that amid so many troubles they were a consolation to me. The affection and interest you show, and above all hearing that you all share in my sufferings — I assure you I at once felt a sweet mixture of pleasure and pain.

  2. My dear, if you could see how different Rome is from what you imagine! There are no festivities; everything is sadness and mourning. The Holy Father always in his prison; good people live in constant fear of being killed at any moment; the earth is bathed [with] the blood of priests; the delegations that come to surround the Holy Father are left [exposed] and booed, as are foreign Religious.2 All they have done is hold penitential processions of women and of men, but all in silence. Then great prayers. Everything hidden and silent; the convents of the Poor Religious all living in fear.3 Demonstrations by Jews every moment — my God, how painful!

  3. Our affairs drag on so long that they make me agonise; what tribulation! Pray, pray; only prayer can find a way out.4

  4. I want to know whether you have bills,5 because you never mention

them. I hope you have none. It would be good for you to visit the Countess now and then.6

Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and you in particular, filling you with his choicest blessings.

I am your very Poor Mother

Rosa

It is not advisable for the girl with scrofula to go to Sampierdarena, since her illness is infectious. Warm encouragement to trust in Providence and to live poverty with dignity, pride and joy. No attention should be paid to rumours against the Institute. Rather, pray, imploring God's abundant blessing on all.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I reply to your letter about the girl, about sending her to S. P. D'Arena. It cannot be done: I fear she may pass the illness on to the others, and in a spirit of charity I cannot allow it.1 Rather find some other means, even if we ourselves had to take her to where the others are, all without taking anything. Whatever can be done, try to do it for M. se of everything, but putting her in S. P. D'Arena cannot be done.2

  1. I hear from the Delegate of dal Verme that she will give you a little money. You see, Providence never fails. Courage! See whether you can get a little firewood, so that you can do the washing at once and send your nuns to the dal Verme House to do it together with the postulants.3

  2. As for poverty, which you say you are ashamed of, I don't understand such language: must we be ashamed of what we make a vow of? And with God's help we must try

to put it into practice! Who was poorer than Jesus? And if we are to imitate him, we must always be in stables and caves. You are neither in caves nor even in stables.4 If they say to you, «How poor you are!», [answer]: «Madam, this is our treasure, and if we had the income of Croesus our dwellings would still be these, because the vow we make requires it; but believe me, we are very happy».5

4. In your letter you told me about the tall tales being said in town, which the Father is supposed to have written; they are all inventions, for nothing of what you wrote me is true: all tall tales, inventions. If they want to amuse themselves, let them, and meanwhile we will laugh, for I assure you they only made me laugh.6 Amid so many real troubles and tribulations, these make us think seriously and pray hard before God, that he may be merciful to us and pour out his blessings on us with a generous hand.7 Greet all the daughters for me, and God bless them all, giving them strength and the spirit of the holy Rule, and bless you in particular, as this poor

M. R. of yours wishes for you.

She says she is very pleased with her conduct. She hopes nothing will arise to prevent her return to Piacenza on 3 July. She will bring medals and crucifixes blessed by the Holy Father.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My blessed daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Your conduct and your way of acting are very dear to me and I am delighted; carry on always like this. By God's mercy I hope to leave Rome on Monday of next week, the 3rd, and by the middle of that week I shall be in Piacenza.1

  2. I am laden with medals and crucifixes blessed by the Holy Father for you. The crucifixes are lovely; I managed to get them all alike; and for the Superiors a little something they will treasure.

  3. Pray that no more hitches arise, so that I can return and my departure is not diverted.2

  4. Have you been to the Countess? Was she pleased? Go often, for charity's sake.3 Don't write to me in Rome any more; address everything to Piacenza.

God bless you together with all the others

P. M. R.

5. I am sending you two little portraits, one for you and the other for Signora Caterina;4 you put a little saliva on it and stick it to the clock; it has gum on the back — my greetings to Signora Caterina. It is a very, very good likeness; the Holy Father to the life.

She writes her the instructions to be read to the nurses on their conduct with the sick they nurse at home. She commends a sister who is unwell.1

A.M.F.2

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. You will read this letter to all of them: gather them and read it aloud, asking whether they understand each point. Daughters, the report you are to give before the Priest Don Luigi must be like this: two by two, together with the Mother Delegate, and what you are to tell him is this: whether, for example, something has happened in that house concerning the occupants or the patient; how the patient is, what you did for her, provided these are things that do not touch on modesty.3

  2. Then, whatever you may have done against your holy Rule must be told only to your Delegate, one at a time; and if she wants to hear you together, you will go together as she directs.4

  3. None of you is to pull faces before Don Luigi, letting him notice that you would have something to say; no, give your report naturally. Now, if you have started going one at a time, continue to go one at a time together with your mother Delegate.

  4. As for the senior in vocation, who is to act as the first with the

sick, this is her duty: to stay up in the first part of the night, and to watch the time when she is to withdraw from the patient for prayers and meditation. If she has a sister who knows little and understands nothing, she must, without the patient noticing, teach her everything else she is to do.5

  1. As for the second, her duty is to stay by the patient's bed; she must do everything the patient needs without asking the other's permission; she must not, for instance, tell the other each time she has to give her a drink, food, etc., etc.; she must do this without asking the other, attentive to the medicines; but when one sits down, she first tells her sister everything she has done up to that moment; likewise how she is to give her the medicines and when to prepare her food, and then they will go together, if the patient can do without someone at her bedside — not, for example, if she were seriously ill and there were a danger of her throwing herself out of bed; so too when you take over from each other6 it is good to tell the others everything they must do and give. These points seem to me very clearly explained; I want to know whether you have all understood me.

  2. I want you to give Sr. A. Annunciata a little undiluted wine at meals or afterwards, as she prefers; it would also be good for her to eat some little thing she likes; if the storekeeper has some little thing, let her give it to her. How is Sr. A. Gerolama?7

  3. Now I urge you very, very much to pray that I may soon finish everything, for it is truly very painful — my God, what tribulations! Only God can give us everything.

  4. I have just received a letter from you and am glad to hear that Providence is helping you. Blessed be God, who mercifully protects you. As for the Portapuglia girl, you can take her to her aunt; who knows, she may look after her; point out to her that we are poor; it would be good if you went yourself.8

The Lord bless you; believe me always

Your P. M. Rosa

9. As for Signora Airenta, I don't know what you are writing to me about;9 write and tell me what it is, more clearly. It is not true that we are celebrating here; on the contrary, the city is in mourning.10

Her departure has been postponed by a few days. She is in very poor health. Advice about two postulants.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us. My daughter,

  1. I was slow in answering your letters; the reason is that I had to stay in bed and am still far from well.

  2. Our departure had finally been fixed for Monday, and now yesterday came another counter-order, putting it off until Wednesday of next week, that is, the 5th of next month.

  3. I long to be in your arms; I feel ill and deprived of everything; the anguish that weighs on me most is that usual agony which weakens me and makes me die. My daughter, how many troubles, how many hardships, how many torments!

  4. My God! Ah, accept them, and may they all benefit your work and be deducted from my purgatory!

  5. So I hope, with God's help, to be with you on Friday, or on Thursday at midnight; you will have a telegram then.1

  6. I was so pleased to hear about our new benefactresses; for charity's sake, tell no one, but see that they come for Saint Anne's feast, and cherish them; when I come I will pay them a visit of thanks.

  7. Everything else is fine; you will have given the Delegate something out of this, and so she will no longer despair.2

  8. As for the postulant with the 300 fr., see whether it is not a temptation of the devil; have her make 5 days' retreat and sep-

arate her from the others, and then you will see — if you think fit. Has the other one from Genoa settled down? I hope so, for this will be pure temptation.3

9. Greet Defilippi4 for me, and all the Religious. They must have prayed very little, for, my dear, I obtained nothing.5 Goodbye; the Lord bless you and all the others. Tell the Delegate6 that I am not writing to her any more because it costs me too much, feeling very ill, with such exhaustion that even my arm aches. Goodbye

[your P. Mother]

In two letters she has written about the postulant from Genoa: she should tell her to be at peace, that if she really wants to leave she will get all her belongings back, but that she should pray, because it is a temptation. She should prepare the girls for Confirmation and pray that the Mother may obtain what the house needs and return as soon as possible. She should keep everything in order and pay off some debts.1

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My blessed daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have received two letters from you, and in both you speak of the postulant from Genoa;2 tell her in my name to be at peace, that I assure her she will have all her belongings, and that she should drive away her fear of leaving, for it is nothing but a real diabolical temptation. Let her make a novena to Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, and everything will vanish, and let her thank God every day for the beautiful grace he gave her of a vocation.

  2. My dear, you ask me so many little things for which you need not wait for my opinion and obedience; as for going to Signora Rocca, by all means go, and indeed try to keep her always happy.3 Tell Sr. A. Bernardina privately to try to build up her strength, for soon it will be time to work.4

  3. You must also prepare all the girls for Confirmation and see that there is a good number of them; take this in hand.

  4. I let you know that Father Agostino will come with me; I must also tell you that for the feast of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, the girls

must have good dresses and stockings for eight days, since people will be coming.

  1. Pray that I may soon obtain what our poor house so badly needs and so return; otherwise things drag on longer and longer, and I can assure you I am truly distressed to find myself so far away and unable to do anything.

  2. Tell Francesca that I am not writing to her5 because I don't feel very well, and Carlottina too has been crying for ten days with her teeth.

  3. I am having someone write at this moment to the Delegate of S. P. D'Arena about the postulant's belongings,6 and if unfortunately she has had the shoes given to the little girls, you are to have a pair made for her at once; try to help her get over this annoyance by keeping her cheerful.

  4. See that the Chapter room is in good order, and the nurses' room, that is, the school; as for the girls' schoolrooms, you mention whitewashing: do as you think best; indeed I am pleased to have those rooms whitewashed.7

  5. The 400 F. you will receive from the postulant, take at once to Cervi; and if the one with 600 comes, give those to the miller.

10. Let us hope that the dear Sacred Heart of Jesus will pour out his graces on us, and his providence on all the houses. Greet all the religious for me and urge them to pray. Goodbye. I am your poor

Mother Rosa

  1. God bless you and all the others, pouring out his abundant blessings on you. I have just received more letters from you, and it is a real consolation to me to hear about the nurses and the seriously ill patients. Blessed be God!

  2. My dear daughter, everything you have done is fine; carry on. You say your letters will bore me — how could that be? Write to me, for your letters are very dear to me, and I prove it by answering you myself. I am pleased with the girls.

  3. My dear, things drag on so long here that unless God works a miracle it will certainly take some days more. Tell the religious to pray hard.

  4. You ask whether exposition may be held in the morning: yes, it may; exposition can be at the high altar and Mass said at Saint Anne's altar. Volpi is fine; I am pleased.8 Daughter, God bless you and pour out on you abundantly his

gifts, and make you a great saint, and one day, after working here on earth, may we be together rejoicing in Paradise. Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate Mother Rosa

The Father will hand her the note and give her news. She had to stop at Bologna because she was ill.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of Our Eternal Father be with you

  1. You will receive this note from the Father, so that you see what they did to me.2 At Bologna I suffered greatly all night and all day, but all for Jesus. I hope my Eternal Father was satisfied.3

  2. For the moment I have not set out;4 my head aches so. Daughter, learn [to] suffer, and you will taste it in loving.4 Tell the Father everything. Goodbye; the Lord bless you

your Mother

She thanks her for her hospitality. Grateful, she prays for her and awaits her. Her apartment is being prepared to welcome, as an awaited guest, the one who is founding a new house in honour of Saint Anne.

My dearest beloved Sister,

  1. Your gracious hospitality so invigorated me1 that my journey was a happy one; I can tell you it is the first in fifteen years in which I suffered nothing. I never needed orange-blossom water.

  2. I was alone with Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, and with you, who after Paradise hold the place in my mind; and this morning at the feet of my Eternal Father and my dear Mother Saint Anne all my wretched prayers were for you, as were those of the whole Community. Believe me, Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, loves you, loves you so much.2

  3. At this moment your apartment is being prepared; everyone awaits you with immense pleasure and a lively desire to see the one who, like her favourite Daughters, is loved by Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, and is our foundress of a consoling new House; every word of yours echoes in my ear.3 Do you want to know why? In all confidence: when I had the joy of having you near and you, without realising it, spoke to me of works of charity and expressed your desires for the good of others, the expression on your lips was such that it seemed — as it was — driven by that flame of charity which burns in your noble heart.4

  4. I would have very many things to tell you, but the carriage is waiting to take me to the Bishop. Tomorrow I will write again at more lei-

sure; meanwhile be pleased to receive a thousand affectionate wishes from one who calls herself, for life, in Jesus, wholly yours

Sister Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

P.S. The girl Carlottina begs you to accept a thousand thanks together with my own most sincere and grateful ones, and [those] of Sr. A. Vincenza, who with Carlotta kiss your hand a thousand times, and I sign myself your

Humble Servant Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

As soon as she arrived in Piacenza she read the correspondence. She will consult the Prefect and answer her question. She should write if she needs more religious. She is sending the little gifts brought from Rome, since she cannot come until after Saint Anne's feast.

■ A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Last night I had only just arrived in Piacenza, and at midnight I was reading all your letters. This morning I could not reply at once because I thought it best to wait until I had spoken with the Prefect here, to hear what he says about what you ask me in that paper. So I wrote to him at once; he will be here shortly and I will hear what he says.1

  2. As for the coffee, keep one weight for yourself and send the other to S. P. d'Arena, where there are very many girls.2

  3. If you think two more religious could come to you, I would order them sent from S. P. d'Arena, all the more since I hear they have few patients, and I need to send from here in Piacenza some religious who need to take the baths.3 Write to me at once and choose those you see are best suited for Genoa.

  4. I am sending to S. P. d'Arena some little things brought from Rome, blessed by the Holy Father; each will have her name on it. I want to know how many crucifixes the religious are missing.4 I can-

not come before the feast of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, but as soon as the feast is over I will be with you.

5. Serafina writes that the Marchioness Cambiaso has an apartment to let, but if that gentleman offers you one without any rent it would be well to wait.5 Meanwhile find out how much rent she wants. God bless you all, and you in particular

Goodbye; I am your most affectionate Mother Sr. A. M. Rosa

P.S. The Prefect has not come yet, so I think I will send you this letter to relieve your anxiety.

She thanks him for his interest in the Institute. She has visited the House in Ferrara. As soon as it is free the Sisters will go there. The Countess has prepared something for them.

Your Excellency,

  1. I hope you received two poorly composed lines of mine written while I was in Bologna.1 As soon as I arrived in Piacenza I would have written to you again had my poor health not prevented me.

  2. Last night I wrote to His Eminence thanking him for the great favour done me, of which Your Most Reverend Lordship was the promoter.2

  3. Rest assured that this wretched creature and the whole community will always remember you in their prayers as their greatest support.

  4. I went to visit the house in Ferrara. It is very fine, and as soon as its little Priests leave, the Daughters of Saint Anne will go there. What consolation I feel at the mere thought that these creatures will be entrusted to Your Excellency and will find in you a father who will support and comfort them.3

  5. The good Countess4 has already prepared wine and other things for the religious and has promised to look after them.

  6. I commend to you our matter of the Rule and anxiously await a line that will console me.5

  7. Please grant me your blessing, while kneeling at your feet I remain, with the deepest veneration, Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I am sending you a letter from the Father; read it carefully and then do what is written in it regarding this unfortunate creature.11

  2. How grieved I am at everything that is happening in that house!22 My God, what sorrow, what pain!3 The holy Mother must be deeply grieved to have such wicked and unmortified daughters.

  3. Oh, whoever is not mortified cannot be a good Christian; gluttony is truly the monster that drags our perverse nature down to the ugliest obscenities.

your most affectionate M. R.

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I hope you received my letter asking you to send me 1,000 F. I hope you will send them at once, for I need them desperately. My daughter, today I spent a day of anguish over this; I will tell you everything in person.

  2. Tomorrow Gigino leaves with D. Gaetano — imagine!2 Today I went to the Morte;3 and this evening it is already very late.

  3. My blessed creature, for charity's sake don't fret because you are far away; believe me, you are closer to me than when I have you at my side; there is not a moment when my thoughts are not on you, and I keep saying to my God the Father: «Stretch out your right hand over my Sr. A. Vincenza and give her great light, so that she may do everything well; keep her for me as my daughter; but you know, it was you who gave her to me, you must keep her for me».4

  4. I am better; the [toothache] has stopped completely; today I did not stay in bed, even though I walked back from the Morte on

foot; I only had a little stomach ache, but now it has gone, and you see, it is 11 % and I am still writing to you without much trouble.

  1. My daughter, why do you tell me to burn your letter? Are you too afraid I will let others read them? You know well that I never show letters containing anything personal; on the contrary I put them straight into my pocket. How can you, who know my ways so well, be afraid? I will not suppose such carelessness of you.5

  2. Go to Maria's as often as you can, for that way you may find something out. Listen, everything must be left in God's hands; you can tell her: «Maria, the Mother knows you give work to the Sister of Charity; she would ask you to provide some for the Daughters of Saint Anne too, but she doesn't want to take anything away from those Sisters, [only] the surplus». But do this without insisting, in a general way; for the rest, let us leave everything to Jesus, and we shall see that he will do it all well.6

  3. I hope I shall find something comforting about the House and the accounts in your other letters. I wrote to the Delegate that you are to bring me the inventory of everything, including the nuns' wardrobe; don't trust anyone; look yourself in the drawers, in the nuns' boxes, at the linen.

  4. For fear these may go astray, I am sending them to Castelletto — I don't trust the post. I close because it is too late.7

Goodbye; believe me yours for ever

Affectionate Mother Rosa

May God pour out his gifts on you most abundantly, blessing you.

P.S. On second thought, try to arrange things with Maria so that in the end she gives no work, because it would not be suitable now that they have such good work.8

She first presents the social aims of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and the nursing and educational service the Religious provide in Piacenza, Sampierdarena and Genoa. In Genoa 12 Sisters, lodged in a few rooms offered by a pious lady, nurse many sick people at home, but this small number is not enough for the growing requests for nursing, nor can it be increased, since the Institute lacks the means to obtain premises. She therefore asks the Municipality to assign it a suitable building.1

Most Illustrious Mayor,

1. Rosa Gattorno, foundress and Superior of the charitable Institute called the Daughters of Saint Anne, respectfully sets forth to Your Most Illustrious Lordship:

That this Institute has as its object: 1. Nursing the sick of both sexes, at home and also in Hospitals.

2. The education and instruction of the children of the poor, especially abandoned girls at risk. 3. Home nursing is provided to all who request it, night and day, by two Sisters at a time. The service is entirely free. In the patients' homes the Sisters may not accept even a sip of coffee. 4. Girls taken in from the streets, or who come to the Institute in any other way, are maintained, educated and taught free of charge and are trained in weaving linen and cotton.2 The benefit of instruction is extended to boys up to the age of 12.

  1. That this Institute, founded in 1866, has met with such public favour that it already has two Houses in Piacenza, one in Ferrara and another in Sampierdarena. That another, provisional House has existed for six months in Genoa, in a few rooms offered in her own home by a pious Lady,3 where for lack of space no more than 12 nursing Sisters can be accommodated.

  2. That this small number is already insufficient for the many requests for nursing made by families of this city who wish to avail themselves of their services.

  3. That to meet the ever-growing demand of the population, and also to give the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne a permanent home in this city, larger premises would be needed that could be relied on for the future; but the scant means at the Institute's disposal — it lives entirely on the alms it receives day by day from pious benefactors — do not allow it to obtain them.

  4. In these circumstances the humble petitioner, earnestly desiring to establish this useful Institute permanently in her native City, sees no other way of achieving her aim than to turn, as she does with full confidence, to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, who so worthily represents its generous and pious population, to ask you to grant her for this purpose the use of one of the premises owned by the Municipality or, failing that, to come to her aid with an annual subsidy.4

  5. The evident public usefulness of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne; the general goodwill it has won wherever it has become known; the favour and protection it has received from the government, which recognised in it the legal character of a charitable foundation; the proverbial piety and munificence of this illustrious City; the generosity with which the city Administration provides for the needs of all its charitable Works, old and new alike — all give the petitioner the most well-founded hope that her humble petition will be kindly granted by Your Most Illustrious Lordship, the Municipal Executive and the City Council.

[Most devoted Rosa Gattorno]

Being in Piacenza, she has no time to write. She should arrange for Sig. Squarzoni to ask for more Religious; she has them ready. She leaves for Genoa the next day.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My beloved daughter,

  1. I have just received your letter; I am replying by stealing a little time from my prayers — and now they are calling me to the door.

  2. Daughter, remember I am in Piacenza, where I no longer have time to breathe, and always unwell.1

  3. My dear, try to get Squarzoni to send for religious; I have them ready;2 and I am always with you; at every moment I press you to the Heart of the holy Mother, that she may make you hers, holy, and great in Heaven.

Goodbye; I will write to you tomorrow evening from Genoa; address your letters to me at Castelletto, where I am going.3

Goodbye. The Lord bless you. I am yours for ever

Mother Rosa

She arrived in Genoa with a headache that still persists. She is at her parents' house because her mother is unwell and her father is in bed with a broken arm. She will soon go to the sisters.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. My journey was fair, accompanied only by the headache that is still with me. Today I am at mamma's, because last night Maddalena and Sr. A. Serafina1 were at the station with the carriage to take me home, as mamma is ill; and as soon as I got off, in the carriage they told me: «We have something to tell you about your papa: he fell and broke an arm». On the eve of All Saints he was on his feet, fell and broke his arm.

  2. Patience; God's will be done. Now he is in bed and cannot move.

  3. If a letter comes from the Frenchwoman in Rome, telegraph me at once.2 This evening I go to Castelletto, and tomorrow I will try [...]3

Greet all the sisters for me and believe me your Affectionate Mother Rosa. God bless you

She prays the Father to fill her with graces to guide the Daughters of Saint Anne well. She should keep to the Rule for the Delegate. About a sister unsure of her religious life, she suggests suitable words to clarify and correct her conduct. Some advice.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter,

  1. I have just received a letter from you with so much good news; I bless God for it, and bless you, my dear, that this most merciful Father may fill you with graces and gifts, with light, so that you can guide the Daughters of Saint Anne well.

  2. Now to the Religious' faults; I weep over them at the feet of the holy Mother, and you must try to put into practice the Rule for the Delegate, administering the penances that Rule lays down for the faults committed.

  3. Then about Sr. A. Angelica, listen: if she again talks to you about wanting to leave and saying she was better in the world, answer her: «Sr. A. Angelica, now I tell you that I will hear no more such talk, and you oblige me to tell you that the world is always ready to receive you and our Institute ready to give you back every last centime of what is yours. I warn you that the first time I hear such words I will send you away immediately, take your habit from you and send you to Genoa; and never again say that you want to throw yourself out of the window. This is a scandal, and after

such words I can no longer allow you to receive Holy Communion. Make up your mind; the holy Mother Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, keeps no one against their will; indeed, those who do not do their duty well are sent away at once. Read the Rule and pray God to give you perseverance». That, my daughter, is how you must act.

4. Don't be1 afraid for Sr. A. Camilla, for it will be nothing; give her chamomile compresses when that trouble comes on; they go on the feet. I very much want you to send for religious soon.2 Goodbye. I can't do more for now, as I am too busy; one day you will hear. Goodbye; the Lord bless you and all the others

I am your Affectionate M. Rosa

She went to Novi to visit Alessandro, who is well. Then, on arriving in Genoa, she had to go to her parents' house, both being ill. Her brother-in-law Giovanni Argenti will visit her with his little daughter. She should receive him with every courtesy and kindness.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday I arrived in Novi at a few minutes past 10 and found Alessandro very well and happy;1 I stayed until 4, then went to Genoa, where I found Sr. A. Serafina and Maddalena at the station with the carriage: mamma was ill, and they had come to tell me that papa had broken his arm in a fall on the eve of All Saints.2 I am writing to you from papa's bedside, on my knees.

  2. I left word in Piacenza that as soon as you send for the Religious, they are to be sent to you.3

  3. Now I let you know that one of these days my brother-in-law Argenti4 will come to see you; show him everything and ask him to stay for lunch and dinner; please receive him well, as he deserves; if you had some little thing for dear Mari, his little daughter, I am sure he would appreciate this welcome, and it will do our house great good. Show him everything at its best, including the Countess's apartment, and speak well of her to him.5 This is Giovanni Argenti.

  4. Are you pleased? I have always written to you in my own hand; write to me at Castelletto, where I shall go this evening. Sr. A. Vincenza is

copying out for you the book for the nursing lessons, and then I will send it.6 I hope you received a parcel with the books and the Rule to take to the Monsignor Vicar. If he comes to visit you and says anything about the Congregation, write and tell me and answer him as you think best; and if he wants me to come to see it begin,7 I shall be ready at once. If you see Monsignor, give him my warm regards, and also(?) Signor Squarzoni.8 I close to post this. God bless you; believe me your affectionate M. Rosa. God bless them all; greet them for me.

The Parish Priest of the Cathedral has told her he intends to establish the Congregation of Christian Mothers, and she has written to him and sent him the Saint Anne manuals. She should be able to tell him something about it if he visits. Advice on running the house. From now on she will not write so often; it is not good to foster such a habit.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I received another letter from you saying you had not understood. I think I told you before leaving that Parish Priest Ferri1 of the Cathedral wanted to set up the Congregation of Christian Mothers under the title of Our Lady of Sorrows and Saint Anne; so if he comes — I had someone write to him and sent him the manuals of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate2 — I don't know whether he has replied.

  2. You are right that I never finish my sentences; you know, I am always being interrupted. As for the little girls and catechism, do as you think best; as for age, certainly not under five. You did well about the school, do you understand? Indeed, for the future, try to think of acting like the ingenious ant, for charity's sake.

  3. My dear, if you knew how many troubles we have on all sides! You ask whom I left as acting Superior in Piacenza: it is Sr. A. Concetta.3

  4. From what the Countess writes, she is not keen to increase the number of Nuns; patience. If Sig. Squarzoni manages it, let us leave everything to God.4 Whatever you are given, keep it well guarded, do you understand? You will say: «Today the mother uses a curious expression», but you must not take it in its material sense, but rather...5

  5. It is not good for me to spoil you by writing so often; such habits later become vices, and a vice can no longer be removed. Yesterday you spoke to me of melancholy and pointed out something because you fear I do not...6 — a child, a real child! I have no more time; it is already late and I still have to say the rosary.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you and all the others; have them pray, for I need it desperately your Affectionate Mother Rosa Gattorno

She blesses God that the house is doing well. She thinks it should go on accepting girls, at least until the number reaches 150. In Genoa no suitable premises can be found and they live amid many difficulties. She is ready to give it all up if God so wills. The girls should pray. She will send Sr. A. Carmelina's teaching certificate as soon as possible.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received a letter from you — I have been at Castelletto since last night —1 with one from Alessandro inside, and there was one for you, which I enclose.

  2. I hear the good news of the house and bless God, the author of all our good; he alone is everything, my daughter. I also note the number of girls; you say you have stopped [admitting them]. I would be in favour of continuing to accept them until there are at least 150. That would be my wish. As for the sick, try to find a way of having the dear Countess asked to send for at least two more religious, so that you will be at least 12.2 Let us hope the Lord finds a way for that matter we spoke of, not...3

  3. My dear, here I am in a sea of tribulation: no house can be found, we have every kind of setback, and the least of them — and there are many — are the persecutions. I keep saying to my God: «Give me light to know whether you want this house, or else, if

it does not please you, I shall be ready at once to take everything away;4 I don't know what to think; the anguish is such that I could not describe it».

  1. You returned Gigino's letter without renewing the stamp, so I had to pay 30 centimes.5 I mention it for your guidance.

  2. My dear, listen, have all the little girls you have pray a little, so that our dear Countess may be freed from the gadfly you know of,6 before they go home, which would be at 11%. Have them start a short novena to the holy Mother to obtain this grace at once, and let them all say aloud three times: «Mother of the Immaculate, hear us»!

  3. My God! Believe me, this is a great sorrow for me. You did well to write everything to our dear Countess; always do as I told you. Write her everything and often, giving her all the news.

  4. I would like to know something about those who stayed in Bologna. I hear about Sr. A. Carmelina; right after lunch I will send to S. P. D'Arena, and if it is there I will send it at once; meanwhile I think you could send the application, saying in a little note that I am awaiting the certificate because the sister left it in another house; believe me, it would be good to do this so that no hitch arises.7 I am sending the letter to the Father. For charity's sake, keep an eye on that careless Sr. A. Daria.8 I say nothing of my health, for it is the same as ever.

Goodbye for now. The Lord bless you and the others, whom please greet warmly.

I am your Affectionate Mother Rosa

She sends Sr. A. Carmelina's documents. She hopes to settle the next day the rental terms for the Community's new premises. A prayer to the Sacred Heart for the sisters, especially for her daughter Adelaide.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Here are Sr. A. Carmelina's papers;2 so I am writing to you again — two letters today; too rich, as Carlotta says.

  2. Tomorrow I hope to settle the house; pray as I wrote to you this morning.3

  3. It is too late to write more; I am so busy in mind and body. Goodbye; urge all the sisters to pray.

  4. Ah, Heart of my Jesus, be moved towards these unworthy creatures, and most of all towards this infamous one, and bless my daughter; fill her with heavenly gifts, especially charity, so that she may become your true bride.

I am your affectionate

Mother Rosa

She receives and answers her letters. She wants to know what the Father said that upset her. She will stay on in Genoa until she can find a larger house for the Sisters. She should take in the widow recommended by the Parish Priest and ask the Superior of the Mother House for the money to pay the butcher's debt.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My dear daughter,

  1. I have just received another letter from you; you can perfectly well address them to Castelletto,1 where I receive them safely; so I received the Father's, just as today you will receive one from the Father together with one from Sr. A. Vincenza for you. Are you pleased to have letters every day? I do indulge my poor little girls, who always want their sweets.2

  2. I hear about the long conference; well, those in need should rightly be fed; I want to know at once what it was the Father said that upset you; write and tell me at once, but clearly, without preambles.

  3. Today I am at papa's; they had3 a very good night, and this evening I go to Castelletto and will stay there a while until I find a place to house these creatures.

  4. Yesterday I read in your letter of the long talk with the Parish Priest;

it would be good if you could get him to give you a bed and then go at once to the dal Verme House to fetch the widow; if you get another, you can take Apollonia, who is always good. It's true she has sciatica, but when she goes out she is always fine.4 Try to send her with someone who has no whims; for the rest, I think you will do so, if you see fit.5

  1. My dear, how many troubles there are here! Only God can remedy them; we are a fine nothing and less than nothing. They have no providence of any kind; I don't know where to turn.

  2. Today I have a stomach ache that is strangling me; I bear it very well, with ease; I seem to have learnt a little by dint of practice. My daughter, if only the Lord would accept these sufferings of mine in discount of my many iniquities. Ah yes, let me say it: the blows this poor Work receives are all the fruit of my infamies. If it so pleases God, let us adore his divine majesty.6

  3. I say nothing about the sisters' faults, because you must speak of these to the Father, and he will remedy everything.7

  4. See that Sr. A. Concetta gives you the money, for I want you to pay the butcher and the other bills.8

Goodbye; the Lord bless you and the others. Believe me yours for ever

Poor Mother Rosa

My dear daughter,

  1. Don't be upset that I didn't tell you what you write about; we certainly had very little time, and besides you know that I report on the houses to the Father instead, and so everything is included.

  2. Don't worry, for charity's sake; why cry? That's for children; come, be cheerful, for I have news: at this very moment I have settled the house and everything is done.1 I can't write at length now; I am writing on my knees at mamma's bedside.

  3. You have done everything well. I want you to go to the Verme house2 and have that stove which used to be in the school well packed in straw, with its iron pipe, carefully so that it doesn't break or get damaged; send it to me at S. P. D'Arena addressed [to] Don Luigi Decavi;3 understood? Good; try to send it at once, for I need it.

Goodbye; I will write again this evening. I am ever your most affectionate Mother Rosa. God bless you together with all

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received your letter saying the certificate has arrived and the teachers are angry; don't be afraid, stay calm, and tell Sig. Squarzoni to say nothing to the dear Countess, for she is so sensitive it might upset her, and it is of no importance.1

This is the third letter she writes to her. Her hands seem to be losing their strength. She blesses God for it, a most delicate and tender Father to her, unworthy as she is. She has a thorn in her heart, caused by seeing her daughter's behaviour, which shows how little she loves God. She asks God to make that heart his own for ever.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter, wholly ours

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today — or rather just now — I received your last letter, the third since I arrived; now a line in my own hand, though it costs me much effort; and believe me, these are the only lines I have written in my own hand since I have been here — apart, of course, from those to the Father.

  2. God seems to want to grant me the grace of my hands becoming powerless, so that I can no longer write. How good our Eternal Father is, who satisfies our desires, especially with this ugly slave of his, truly as loathsome as a rotting corpse; O «dear Jesus, I reek so with the stench of my infamies, and yet, my Good, you still deign to be with me and come into me».1

  3. Listen, I have a thorn, and do you know what it is? It is seeing how little you love God. You will say: «How can you know that?». Here is how, my dear daughter: your lack of patience in adversity, in small acts of self-denial, in the sufferings of your

state, your lack of resignation to the Divine will; those fits of temper as soon as the prospect, even at a distance, of giving up the milk of sweetness appears; at once, regardless of offending God, one gets upset, gives scandal, talks loudly in time of strict silence.2

  1. My God! Do these things not say plainly that this heart is empty of your love and still swathed in flesh? Consume it, consume it, and make it wholly yours for ever!3

  2. Love, and then do what you will, and you will do everything well and please God.4

I am your Affectionate Mother Rosa

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My blessed daughter,

  1. I received both your letters, and only now do I have a little time, while I scold everyone who isn't doing things right.1

  2. Now to you; listen: earlier I forgot to tell you and write that you should tell Sig. Squarzoni to have the Church windows made as in all Churches, high, and not like ordinary house windows.2 Then, if the Countess has plates3 bought for feeding the girls, try to buy ones like those in Piacenza, and the glasses too. I think the best day to give them the lunch would be the second day of Christmas, or else New Year's Day.

  1. As for Daria, I hear everything, but God will soon remedy it.4
  1. Here is the address of the house, where at last we have been living for three days. My dear, what toil! It is very nice: Santa Maria di Castello No. 8, second floor.

Goodbye. Greet all the sisters for me, and receive a thousand embraces in Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, your Poor Mother Rosa G.

God bless you and all the others. Today I have an endless headache. For charity's sake, have the little girls pray that that ugly business, you know, may all be over. Poor Countess — you understand me.5

In the Houses of Genoa, Sampierdarena and Piacenza she found order and harmony. They should be grateful to the Lord, who has provided well for them, and ask his forgiveness and grace to amend.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Have Sr. A. Giovanna hear these lines.1

  2. Daughter, do you remember the promises you made me before I left? That you would be very good, would not talk and would disturb no one; so why start breaking so holy a rule as never mentioning to the Confessor the affairs of your religious house? If you have something to complain about, you must write to the Superiors; only sins are to be told to the confessor.2

  3. Ah, what wretched tongues, which continually wound my breast, says the Saint!3 And this poor mother of yours, whom you boast so much of loving, when instead you wound her soul with a thousand-bladed knife — O unhappy ones, what are you doing?

  1. Remember that you force the Superiors to use the whip to keep Saint Anne's flock clean!5

  2. How it pains me to have to say this word! I can only tell you that since yesterday I have had a stabbing pain in my head because of you, so that I find no rest and cannot even lay my head down for a little relief.

  3. If only God would accept my pain and sufferings in discount of your enormous faults.

  4. To you, Superior. Make these words of mine well heard, and calmly and peacefully send those who will not submit back to the House immediately, without further ado. So the holy Mother wills.

  1. My daughter, take courage, for charity's sake; Saint Anne will see to everything.

  2. I have visited the two houses at S. P. D'Arena and Genoa; I can only tell you that I found such order and harmony that it is truly consoling to be in those communities; likewise here in the main house and in the house of the Morte I can find nothing to grieve me; everything is going very well.8
