She explains the tenor of her previous letter, which concerned the Sisters. Advice on a Sister's health. She will take her to Piacenza and, if necessary, send her home. She has nursing sisters ready to send to help in Ferrara but cannot unless the Countess asks for them.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I have just received a letter from you full of pain and sadness.1 My daughter, I can't understand how you, with your ability, could so misinterpret my letter, in which I told you to have it read to the Community. There was nothing for you in it but words of encouragement.

  2. I had to write it because of what you had written about Sr. A. Giovanna and Sr. A. Angelica. Now I hear this is the effect of illness.2 You can advise her to let leeches be applied to the anus; they will do her a lot of good, as she is at the change of life. Certainly the blood could play tricks on her; and then, as soon as she has regained her strength,3 we will take her to Piacenza.

  3. After the Immaculate Conception I am coming to Bologna and will then take her with me to Piacenza, or she can do as she thinks. If she wants to leave at once, she will be satisfied; read her these two lines; and at once foot baths and leeches.4

  4. And you, read carefully what I write, otherwise it drives one mad;

I was not speaking to you but to the sisters, following what you had written to me.5 God permits this for my sins; patience is needed!

  1. I am sending you Gigino's letter which you sent me; it is for you. Courage, my daughter; why get so upset?

  2. Listen, along with consolations there must also be bitterness, otherwise I would fear it was not God's work. You have no external troubles, so God allows you to have internal ones; these are certainly the most painful, but courage, and forward without losing heart;6 let us put everything in the hands of Providence; this good God will calm everything.

  3. These few days pass quickly, so be of good heart; everything will be settled. As for the sisters you ask for, the Lord would have to speak to the dear Countess's heart; then she would ask for more and I would send them to you; speak to Squarzoni.7 For the Immaculate Conception there is a clothing of 9 Religious, all angels with a true vocation; I don't think I have ever had another like it; and then I will send them to you, provided the dear Countess allows.

  4. Tell Sr. A. Angelica again to get everything ready, for she will come away with me, and I assure you that as soon as she is here I will send her away without fail. Let the Sisters hear this privately, so that they see all are treated alike, and that even if she were a scholar or a princess it would be the same.8

  5. The holy Mother wants observance; a member that is not subject to the body must be cut off. I assure you that I am exactly the same towards everyone, with exactly the same affection for all; only, after every attempt has been made and one has suffered as much as is humanly possible, one must tear from one's heart the creature who, sadly, is clearly beyond remedy.

10. Goodbye, my dear; again, take courage and don't grieve. God wants to test us in everything; for charity's sake don't be afraid; if you see she won't calm down, tell Squarzoni the sister needs treatment, take her to Bologna, put her on the train for here, and you go back to Ferrara.9

Goodbye; I am ever your

affectionate Mother

She explains the conditions and arrangements the Daughters of Saint Anne follow in their hospital service.1

Most Illustrious Gentlemen,

1. I send Your Most Illustrious Lordships the information you wish to have:

  1. For that Hospital the Sisters cannot be fewer than five, since a cook, a wardrobe-keeper, a portress and two nurses are needed. The wardrobe-keeper will of course help the nurses when there are seriously ill patients to watch over, since, as Your Lordships know, we do all services for the sick, even the lowliest, for no women servants are employed; we alone undertake all the work of the Hospital.

  2. The stipend to be assigned to each sister is L. 450; if the Hospital supplies oil and firewood, the stipend will drop to only L. 400.

e) As for the maintenance of the patients in all other respects, this system is followed:

The Administration gives the Superior a passbook, or issues vouchers for the butcher, baker and grocer. For other small expenses the Superior keeps a special register in which she records all the small expenses needed for the patients, such as eggs, ice and so on. At the end of each month this book is checked by the President of the Hospital, who then gives the Superior a payment order for the sum spent plus an amount as petty cash.

2. The conditions set out above, which I present to Your Lordships, are entirely exceptional; so much so that in all the Hospitals we serve, the Superior, who is paid the same, has no other duty than direction, whereas in yours she would also act as wardrobe-keeper, which would be to your Administration's advantage. Note too that in the other Hospitals, if we do not receive firewood and oil, we get L. 500, and 450 otherwise.

3. I therefore ask Your Lordships to keep this confidential should other Congregations be approached, since we cannot repeat such exceptions.

With my respects, I remain Your Most Illustrious Lordships'

most devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She urges her to love Jesus and promises to send her the finished dress; she will have grandfather buy the watch and will bring it to her.1

My Carlotta,

  1. Love Jesus very much, your only thought, my daughter; Jesus, wholly your beloved bridegroom.

  2. Tomorrow I will send you the dress, which is finished. I spoke to grandfather about the watch, and tomorrow, when I go to Genoa again, I will see that he buys it for you; I will bring it to you myself.

Greet for me the Superior, Sr. A. Maria Vincenza and the Superior of S. Pier d'Arena.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you every hour, every moment

your poor M. Rosa

She apologises for not writing, gives news of her work and health, and expresses her gratitude. The sisters are growing in number, are in demand and work hard. Fr Tornatore is preparing to send the Rule to Rome. She asks him to obtain 40 crucifixes blessed by the Holy Father for the Sisters.

A.M.F.

My Father Agostino,

  1. Neither dead nor alive, but somewhere between the two, I still wander this earth. Believe me, first of all, that my silence had no other cause than my health, as I wanted to write to you in my own hand.1 For some time now I have practically lived on the railway, and in the couple of days I stay put the affairs of this Institute are so many and so great that my little brain cannot hold them.2 My Father Agostino, truly I tell you, not a day passes without this wretch mentioning you.

  2. Now I am in Bologna, as you will see from the date, and tomorrow in Ferrara. My God, this cold takes my breath away; for two days I have been very ill, and believe me it costs me no small effort, but I do it just as gladly.

  3. Speaking with you, Father Agostino: the gratitude I feel towards you is unequalled, and I would reproach myself if, finding an occasion to show it, I did not; my God will surely give me cause to do so.3

  4. I hear that times in Rome are going from bad to worse: dear holy Mother, protect this fellow worker in your immense vineyard — truly immense.

  5. On the feast of the Immaculate Conception I was in Piacenza and there was another Clothing of 9 Religious. If you could see how they are growing and how much they are in demand — it is astonishing. I won't tell you about the work done by those of the Morte House with the smallpox patients, for in Piacenza it is raging beyond measure, and the demand for our nurses is beyond words. The Municipality wanted to give me another house, but I refused it because I didn't like it; and they were about to give me the Capuchin convent,4 which I don't yet know whether I shall accept, as the necessary expenses would be too great.

  6. These days the Father is working to send the Rule to Rome, as Father Manfredini wrote to us.5

  7. Now, Father Agostino, I would like a great favour: to send me 40 Crucifixes like those you bought for me when I was in Rome; tell me the cost and I will send it by money order, for I need them badly, having so many religious without one, and none to be found here; and also, if I could have — but without great inconvenience to you — a relic of Saint Anne. If you think fit to have the Crucifixes blessed by the Holy Father, they will be all the dearer to us.6

  8. Father Agostino, a word for me to the dear Child, for I need it. Commend me a little to Father Bonaventura; ask him to send me some fine word, for I need it.7

  9. Carlottina is still with her grandparents and is very well. When I was in Genoa at mamma's we talked so much about you, Father Agostino. I told mamma about the meals you brought me every day, and how I saw you as the angel of Providence God had provided so that I would not catch a fever or anything else. My God! Bless him, and may your blessing be so abundant that it pours the choicest blessings on my Father Agostino.

My Father Agostino, write and tell me you understood the reason for my silence, and meanwhile bless me and believe me always, on earth and in Heaven, your most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

She should send the enclosed letter to the Father and ask him whether two postulants may be assigned to nursing the smallpox patients.1

In haste, my dear daughter Francesca.

  1. Please make sure the letters to the Father are sent safely. For charity's sake, have them pray. Tell the Father I would be in favour, in order to satisfy the smallpox patients, of taking postulants too: the stout older one and the other strong little one. Those two seem to me very suitable. Have their beds brought and let them sleep in one part of the dormitory.

  2. On such occasions one must not worry about so many things. We shall have more merit. God sends us bread; we must know how to eat it to grow strong.2

  3. So tell the Father at once. If you think fit to go there, you can take a carriage as far as there,3 which costs only a franc; pay it so no one notices, and walk back; that way you speak to him, and if he says yes, go at once to the dal Verme house on the Father's orders to fetch the postulants.4

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me always your most affectionate M. Rosa

If she buys books and paper for the Ferrara house, she should get a supply for her own school too. If help is needed with the smallpox patients, she should take two more Sisters and postulants from the Mother House.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received both your letters together. I hear all your news, and about the accounts. Blessed be God. Listen: when you go to get the books and paper, get a supply for yourself too.

  2. I hope you received my letters, and about taking the postulants at the Morte. If you see you don't have enough, go and take Sr. A. Agnese and Sr. A. Pacifica and more postulants.2 We must serve these poor plague-stricken people, and you will see that we shall have great merit from God and shall have everything.

  3. Listen, we sent Sr. A. Carmelina's papers to her at once.3

  4. My dear daughter, keep on working. Always write and tell me what Sr. A. Giacomina has done.4

Goodbye; I will write tomorrow. God bless you; I am your most affectionate Mother Rosa

She expresses gratitude for his obtaining the «privileges» for the Chapels of the Institute's Houses; she prays for and wishes him every good and asks his blessing.

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. Unable to write in my own hand, having had a fever for several days, I make the effort to dictate from my bed what gratitude, thankfulness and duty prompt me to say for the trouble you took to obtain those privileges for our poor Chapels.1

  2. May God reward you by granting you a very long life; and believe that this poor daughter of yours, in her prayers, in her paltry works and in her very sufferings, asks the good God of mercies to magnify in his sight what would otherwise be nothing, and to accept it to restore health and long life to our so [dear] Protector; and the whole community, prostrate at Your Eminence's feet, offers you the fervent prayers it has made to God for your well-being.

  3. Deign to bless abundantly one who so eagerly awaits it, hoping to draw strength from it to contemplate the Infant Jesus in the crib on holy Christmas Day.

  4. Bless all the communities too; with it they will surely grow in virtue.

Allow me to kiss the Sacred Purple. I remain Your Most Reverend Eminence's most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

She has recovered her health and attributes it to her daughters' prayers. She has suffered indescribable moral and physical pain in utter solitude, but the Father and Jesus have healed and consoled her. She hopes to obtain the Countess's consent to accept more nursing Sisters in the Ferrara House, whom she is ready to support at her own expense.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My daughter,

  1. To prove to you that I am better, as soon as I got up I am writing to you on my knees, so that you and the others may thank the Most High for leaving me still among you, and that I may have the joy of holding you in my arms, as one day we shall rejoice together in your eternal home.1

  2. I thank you with all my soul for the fervent prayers you have offered for my health, though for [me] more [life] is only a prolongation of the painful prison I am in.2

  3. Yesterday, while I was suffering and even fainting — the last faint, thank God, since Wednesday when I left Genoa; and there too I had 6 very painful days, constant anguish, torment and pains of every kind — yesterday at last at 514 came the last one, and so far I can say none has come since; and only today, after noon, could I get out from under the covers, but extremely weak.

  4. My daughter, the Genoa affair took away what little life I had left;3 listen how it worked on wretched humanity: like a millstone (?) that, coming under the blow, the machine crushes, and it is annihilated; that is how I felt. I understand nothing more than this.4 He willed that I be utterly undone; even the air seemed to help consume me. My God! These are the pains of the damned: they suffer and find no relief; I had comfort from nowhere, wholly deprived of human solace. In my anguish, my dear daughter, I was alone; only my Eternal Father was moved to pity, and my dear Crucifix.

  5. Daughter, yes, the wounds of his wounds are our only comfort; they are the balm that heals our wounds, especially the harsh wounds certain irons inflict on our poor breast; and who but you, my God, can tend them? The gentle touch of his hand makes all pain vanish.5 How dear is this Eternal Father of ours, daughter, and Jesus, who so gladly acts as nurse and is so skilful; he knows how to apply his sweet ointment well and at the right time.

  6. Yesterday your telegram gave me great pleasure; as soon as my suffering was over they told me what it said. Blessed be God; I have had someone write to Squarzoni so that he agrees and also begs the dear Countess to send for more nurses. I hope God will do something. I also told her I would support them at my own expense.6

  7. I add nothing more, for I can bear no more.7 God bless you all, and fill you in particular with graces, as I have asked the dear Child with all my soul.8

Goodbye; ever yours

Affectionate Mother Rosa9

10 She did well to send a copy of the newspaper to Fr. Luigi Decavi (director of the girls at Sampierdarena).

She should not set her heart on praise but seek Jesus alone. The Mother fears that one sister is not sincere and is scheming; she should watch her so that this does not happen. She is sorry to hear that another sister falls asleep while nursing a sick lady at night. She should apologise to the lady and warn the sister to obtain from Saint Anne the grace to stay awake; the others too must be alert when nursing at night, or they will be relieved of the task.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I received your letters together with the newspaper. My God! Ah, my daughter, for pity's sake don't set your heart on the praise of this world; remember it is the plague of our soul.1 Flee, for pity's sake, every thought that might lodge in your mind, and say to your Jesus, our good: «Take these devilish firebrands far from me, for I fear they may burn my soul; you alone and nothing more».

  2. Now I must tell you something in strict confidence. Listen, for several days I have been tormented by a thought — very serious for me — that Sr. A. Daria is up to some scheme;2 I'll say no more; I hope God will give you light to understand me and find out. God grant it is only a fear I have imagined. In any case, watch and

make visits; take her by surprise. For pity's sake, don't let her go out for water; I urge you to be very alert; don't trust appearances, for when a person is engaged in such schemes, you must know that in their outward actions they seem good and full of zeal.

  1. This is to give you a lesson — or rather, allow me to put it this way — since you are still a novice in the world's malice, I need to enlighten you a little.3

  2. Now I don't want you to be at all anxious, for charity's sake, but just at peace; and even if there is nothing, keep an eye on her anyway so that it doesn't happen.4

  3. The Father tells me to let you know he did not mean you must say the chaplet every day for a year, but offer to the Lord the chaplet of the Eternal Father you say on Sundays, for a year, for the Father's intention.5 I hope I have made myself clear.

6. Tell Squarzoni that if Sr. A. Vincenza wrote to him about the sister, it was only to say one thing.

  1. I have just received your letter. For charity's sake — I hear about the sister who falls asleep. Tell her to make a novena to the holy Mother to keep her awake.6 You could go to that lady and politely apologise, promising that in future you will send nurses who will not fall asleep, with a thousand apologies. As for the postulant, tell her no, absolutely not.7

  2. Then tell all the sisters, especially those who fall asleep, that if it happens again they will no longer serve in that task and will be put under observance, and then the Superiors will act.8 What a business! My God!

  3. Tell Ignazia to take care to obtain this grace from God and to be watchful, for this is the mortification the Lord wants of her — to her alone, make clear what has been grieving me so much about this house these days: it was this dreadful failing.9 You did well to send the newspaper to D. Luigi; it arrived in time — all by God's permission.10

God bless all the sisters, and you in particular.

Believe me your Affectionate Mother [Rosa Gattorno]

She answers questions about the behaviour of two sisters, suggesting words and ways to correct them. She should never give way to faint-heartedness and above all practise humility. She regrets hearing that she has treated her daughters impatiently and harshly and urges gentleness and forbearance. A sister in charge of posting letters had told the Superior that the sisters wrote directly to the Mother, and discontent arose. She will write to the sisters. She wants to hear soon that harmony has been restored.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Today I received your letters, including one asking me to reply at once. Here I am, doing so gladly.

  2. My daughter, you must never send the sisters to make adoration outside our chapels; and you will forbid them to go into churches when they are out, except when they must receive Holy Communion because they cannot get back in time for the community Mass.1

  3. The other point is that when Sr. A. Giovanna told you she could not go to that house because it would harm her health, you should have said: «If so, as I believe it is, in view of your age,2 I make this exception».

  4. Then you should have taken her aside and kindly said: «Listen, my daughter, when you have some objection about going to the sick, please do as the holy Rule says; and if it is something you find hard, come afterwards, take me aside and tell me all you like».3

  5. Now to Rosa. When this sister made this objection, you should simply have said: «Sister, remember what the Rule says» — if you were alone; if the girls were present: «Go, I tell you, go».4

  6. Then, on her return, or even before, you should have taken her aside and pointed out her fault: that it was a serious fault to object to the Superior's order, and that, since it had been committed in public, she must do penance in the refectory, asking pardon for the scandal.

  7. Then, when you learnt that they had grumbled, you should have gathered them all and said: «Listen, your conduct is most displeasing to God's heart, and the holy Mother wants reparation from you; since you have all soiled yourselves with this sin, you must all do penance»; and if not all were guilty, gather only those who were, and withhold Holy Communion. A tongue soiled with such a sin is no longer worthy to have Jesus placed upon it.5

  8. And then, strength, and never give way to faint-heartedness,6 but always keep that bearing and composure, joined with meekness and charity, which are the true portrait of the Daughters of Saint Anne. My daughter, for charity's sake let us be humble; otherwise Jesus will humble us. Yes, this [I can] assure you: one act of vainglory, and at once God with his dear hand humbles us to the abyss of our nothingness; one act of humility, and the dear Eternal Father comforts us, making his work shine.7

  9. Dear daughter, I urge you to practise this virtue, and I beg you for the love of God and for the love you say you have for me, for without it I shall not see you run on the way of perfection. Without humility one cannot enter Paradise. My dear, console me by giving me proof [that] you will always practise it and that from now on your chief concern will be to have it deeply rooted in your heart.

10. Listen, I can't dwell on this subject any longer now, for I would never finish. My love for this virtue is too great.

  1. You mention Maria's money.8 Listen, do this: note down the little you spend on her, and when she gives you the 40 F., deduct what you have spent on her and put it to the benefactress's account. You may keep the rest. Do you understand?

  2. Goodbye, my dear; I urge you to economise, for charity's sake; the more I think about it... I think 5 F. a day should be enough; you mustn't fret over this.9

God bless you; believe me always your affectionate Mother

[Rosa Gattorno]

A.M.F.

  1. I continue, because I have just received your letter. My daughter, what are you doing? Don't you see you are killing your holy Mother by dishonouring the Institute? If people hear, if word gets out that the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, are at odds, that the Superior shouts and is impatient, what will Sig. Liberali10 say, what [shall] we [say], my God! You are tearing me apart, daughters. Patience!

  2. Ah, for pity's sake, treat your daughters with more motherly love, without embittering them.11 Ah, take them and calmly tell them, for the love of God, to calm their embittered hearts and be... Be forbearing!

  3. Tell me, what was the point of scolding them so much when they had humbled themselves and asked you to refrain from Communion? You should have urged them not to do it again and kindly told them to calm down. For pity's sake, daughter, set things right with your daughters; tell them to be good, and remember they are poor creatures working for Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.

  4. Daughter, the honours have harmed your heart! You see, you see how true it is that they are the plague of our soul!

  5. Now to the letters to be sent to me. Tell one — and I will write to her too — Sr. A. Domenica, whether she has forgotten what I left word: that she was to take them and send them at once without a word to you.12 She was wrong here, and I want her, for this mistake, to ask the sisters' pardon on her knees at table for three days, saying: «Forgive me, sisters, for failing to do what the Mother had told me and what the Rule requires in my office; I do this penance by the Mother's order». She would deserve to have Communion withheld.

  6. Nor must you rebuke so harshly; for pity's sake, you should have waited and then taken Giovanna aside and said: «Listen, Sr. A. Giovanna, why did you give the letter without a stamp to Paolo?13 If you had asked me, I would have given you a stamp». That's it;

and then kindly say: «You see, this is not the way to behave». To Sr. A. Domenica, when she came to tell you the sisters write to the Mother: «Very well, do your duty. Do you know what the Mother told us? Your job is to seal them and send them to her»; but never let it show that it hurts you, and say: «If they write, I will write too».

19. For pity's sake, daughter, I await a letter from you with good news, saying you are in perfect harmony. Now I am writing to the daughters, to all of them.

I am your affectionate [Mother Rosa]

Before leaving for Nizza to open a new house, she asks his pastoral blessing for herself and the eight Religious. She has received his letter, which filled her with joy.1

Most Reverend Eminence,

  1. I cannot leave [for] Nizza Monferrato2 for a new house of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, without Your Eminence's pastoral blessing; together with the eight religious I prostrate myself at your feet [to] receive it, sure of obtaining from it all the graces I need, and especially the strength I utterly lack.3

  2. Today I received your letter,4 which filled me with joy, finding it full of your blessings, so necessary to my poor soul; and if God deigns to hear me, I hope Your Eminence will obtain all you may particularly desire.

Grant your apostolic blessing to one who humbly remains Your Eminence's

. most obliged Daughter Sr. [Anna M. Rosa Gattorno]

After setting out the Institute's nursing, welfare and educational activities and its spread to several cities, she asks for recognition by the Italian Government.1

Your Excellency,

1. Rosa Gattorno, Foundress and Superior of the charitable Institute called the Daughters of Saint Anne, respectfully sets forth to Your Most Illustrious Lordship that this Institute has as its object:

1. Nursing the sick of both sexes, at home and also in hospitals.

2. The education and instruction of the children of the poor, especially abandoned girls and girls at risk.

  1. Home nursing is provided to all who request it, night and day, by two Sisters at a time. It is entirely free. In the patients' homes the Sisters may not accept even a sip of coffee.

  2. Girls taken in from the streets, or who come to the Institute in any other way, are maintained, educated and taught free of charge and trained in weaving linen and cotton. The benefit of instruction is extended to boys up to the age of 12.

  3. That this Institute, founded in 1866, has met with such public favour that it already has two Houses in Piacenza, one in Ferrara, another in Sampierdarena and a fifth in Genoa.

  4. The evident public usefulness of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, the general goodwill it has won wherever it has become known, and the favour and protection it has received encourage the

petitioner to ask for the Government's approval, so as to be able to serve the good of others more and with greater security.

Confident of obtaining so great a favour,2 she has the honour to remain Your Most Illustrious Excellency's

most humble Rosa Gattorno

She urges respect and veneration for Fr Tornatore. Every day she entrusts her dear little Maddalena to Saint Anne. She has had the consolation of seeing several of her little daughters, whom she cared for and brought up from childhood, become brides of Jesus.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. This evening I received your other letter, in which you mention the silly things you wrote. For pity's sake, daughter, remember the respect and veneration this Mother of yours has for the Superior, seeing in him the image of Jesus. How is it that I cannot instil this holy thing, so dear to me, in you?1

  2. I hear about the little girls. Tell them their conduct consoles me greatly and I will write to them as soon as I can.

  3. Tell Maddalena that, though I don't write to her, I am always her poor Mother who holds her close in the heart of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate; every day I commend her to her and say: «Mother, see these two dear little daughters of mine, who have grown up nourished on your milk of providence; and I, wretched as I am, had the good fortune to see them at my side when small, drinking in the holy teachings of our Catholic religion and becoming true Christians and one day brides of Jesus!».2

  4. What consolation to think that I already have sev-

eral of them who are my adopted, legitimate, spiritual daughters and will one day share eternal joy with me!3

  1. This suffices for everything, being our end, the goal we aspire to. The whole world with its joys is nothing and less than nothing compared with an immensity of heavenly goods.

  2. Goodbye. Greet them all for me, and may God pour out the choicest blessings on all my daughters, and on you especially, my blessed creature. May the lights and graces of the Eternal Father be given you in unequalled abundance.

To my little daughters an embrace in the heart of Jesus, that he may keep them pure and holy for me. Goodbye to all; it is late.

I am your Affectionate Mother Rosa

She is deeply grieved to hear that a sister is gravely ill. She is sorry the sick complain that the nurses do not come to them. She should get this service, so pleasing to God, going again, urging on the sisters at her disposal. Instructions about two girls.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I hear what you tell me about the sister and am deeply grieved; she is the fifth from this house to go to Paradise. What can I say? Only: «God the Father's will be done»!1

2. What grieves me most now is to hear that the sick complain because the nurses don't go to them. Listen, try to do as we told you together with the Father: always send the sisters out, and if that is not enough, they will lose a night, even two or three, as they do in Genoa, where even the cook goes. So you see, if you had done so, you would have satisfied the sick and done something very pleasing to the holy Mother.

  1. Get them moving, and you will see the Saint will give them strength.2

  2. As for Sr. A. Giustina, you can try whether the Genoa air does her good; if not, we will call her from there to Piacenza.3

  3. You say you have no more nurses; well: Sr. A. Redentore, Sr. A. Chiara, Sr. A. Prassede, and now there will be Sr. A.

  1. This morning, as I was coming out of Church, I received your letter about the girl recommended by Sig. Liberti, full of complaints that I don't write.1

  2. Remember that since arriving in Piacenza, being constantly ill, I have written to no one, and unless I am mistaken this is the first letter I have written apart from two lines to the Father.2 My health is very poor and my life is wasting away day by day; this morning I got up at 814 because a Capuchin, my dear brother, came to give me Holy Communion. You see, my dear daughter.

  3. Well, let us leave these stories now and spend a little time with God, and then turn to the affairs of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.   4. And then I want to give you a little lesson on this. My dear, do you know who sweetens all our pain? The love of God! She sets out the charitable works the Institute carries out free of charge, supported by alms, in various places, with evident signs of public appreciation. She stresses the principles behind the Institute's Rule and asks that it be recognised and approved as a work beneficial to society.1

Your Excellency,

1. Signora Rosa Gattorno founded in March 1866 an Institute with the following works of charity.

1. Nursing the sick of both sexes and any condition, in any illness, even in time of epidemic, with continuous care day and night. 2. Service in hospitals.

3. Taking in poor young girls who, lacking sufficient care, are in evident danger of being abandoned to ignorance and vice.

4. Teaching poor girls and little boys free of charge up to about the age of twelve, when they can be sent to public schools or apprenticed to a trade.

  1. The said Lady, considering that these works, and especially nursing the sick, are of such interest and benefit to society, hoped that her Institute would win the sympathy of the places where it was established and that they would gladly contribute alms to its support.
  1. Relying on this hope, she made the first tri-

al in the city of Piacenza, where nursing the sick was so much in demand that after the first house a second soon had to be founded. From there she went on to found houses in Sampierdarena, Genoa, Ferrara and Nizza Monferrato.

  1. The hope was not in vain, for in the Institute's six years of life support has steadily grown. By way of example, in the year 1871 just ended the two houses in Piacenza received more than 23,000 lire in alms, as the account books show, which, together with alms in kind, sufficed to support a hundred or more people.

  2. After this experience, the Lady Foundress asks the government to recognise and approve her Institute as a Work beneficial to Society, so that it may found houses wherever it is wanted, citizens may confidently support it, and it may enjoy all the privileges already enjoyed by other Institutes of a similar nature.1

  3. The moral rules on which the said Foundress has based the honourable standing of the Daughters who make up the Institute are:

1. that all the Houses depend on the Foundress and on her successor;

2. so that the said Daughters may be wholly disinterested and the patient may say he knows he has Mothers at his bedside and not hirelings,

it is a law that neither the individual Daughters nor the Institute ask anything for the care they give; so the cities have nurses ready to serve their sick without incurring any obligation towards them;

3. so that the service may be more complete, they go to nurse in pairs.

7. To distinguish her Institute from others of various names, the Foundress has given it the name Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

The petitioner, trusting to obtain this, remains Your Most Illustrious Excellency's

Rosa Gattorno

The Marquis Durazzo, whose daughter has joined the Daughters of Saint Anne, will ask him for information about the Institute. She reports on the six communities she has recently visited.

Most Reverend Father,

  1. It is a long time since I had the good fortune of receiving your letters with news of your health; I would have liked to write this when I was in Nizza Monferrato, in the new House, but my poor health and so much toil prevented me; believe me, though, Father, that at the Foot of the Altar I have never forgotten you, and very often with your daughters — that little flock I left there — we spoke of you; and on the day the Chapel dedicated to Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, was opened, we spoke of Your Paternity for almost a whole afternoon.1

  2. I now want to tell you something. When I was still in the world — indeed in the last year, after which I left for this House of the Lord — I used to be visited by a young lady, the Marchioness Durazzo, and also by her Father; and from then on this creature always had it in her heart to follow me. She went to the Salesian Sisters to make the holy Exercises, and when they were over she had to leave, because she did not find her home there.2

  3. A month ago she came here to the poor House of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate; she finds everything lovely and adapts very well to our extremely poor life. Now her parents, who were content before, seem a little troubled by what is said in Genoa about this Institute, because it has no income yet, and they fear it may not survive; moreover certain people (all people of God) have fears, or point to Rome, because our Constitutions have not yet been approved.3

  4. Today a fine thing happened: the Marquis Durazzo came and would have liked his daughter to agree to leave; but she — note that she is no longer a child but already 30 years old, which gives her, let us say, some help.4 Having heard us speak of Your Paternity several times, after a long talk alone with her Father she told him to apply to Your Paternity, who would give him all the information about our poor Institute, since you gave us the holy Exercises.5 When this creature told me, I replied: this can only be an inspiration from God; and at the same time I felt it my duty to inform Your Paternity, so that you would know why you will be asked for information about the Institute.

  5. Meanwhile I take pleasure in giving you news of all six Houses. Home nursing is increasing in all of them: here in Piacenza in 1871 it numbered 233; S. Pierdarena over a hundred; Ferrara about twenty; Genoa about a hundred.6 At the Morte House they work hard with the little boys, who number 88, all first-rate.7 In Nizza, as you will know, we have the Hospital, Civic Schools, girls at Risk and Home nursing; on the second night after we took possession two sisters went at once to nurse Countess Castello's Agent, and from the news I had yesterday I hear that patients and calls keep increasing.8

  6. That, my Father, is the report on all your daughters living in those poor Houses. May Your Paternity bless them every day, and this one especially, who is the neediest. At the same time forgive me if I have been tiresome with such long reports; but knowing your charity, and feeling I was in your presence, I told you everything quite frankly.

  7. Asking your pardon again, I kneel to receive your blessing, and remain Your Most Reverend Lordship's

most humble Sr. A. Maria Rosa Gattorno

  3. I look forward to your reply, in which I hope to find acknowledgement of another letter I sent you some days ago.

  4. I hear from the Superior that they still don't have the benches for the school; I realise how much work I left, and from this I see the carpenters have not yet been able to make them. most humble Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

Signor Marchese,

Good Superior,

1. I would say: First: give everyone brown [bread], and then let them eat as much bread as they feel they need;

second: if you notice that someone needs white [bread] because she is suffering too much, give it to her, whether she is a teacher or a nurse;2

third: each week ask anyone you suspect may be suffering in silence how the fast is affecting her and whether she feels she cannot do her work as well as when she was not fasting; make her tell you how things really are, and if you see she is truly suffering, do not allow her to fast.3 As for abstinence, follow the indult in force there, since each Diocese has its own.

2. Before Christmas I asked you for the total of the expenses incurred during the year and of the income; I also wanted to know exactly what the girls' monthly fees are;

how much comes in, and from the work now. For good order all the houses send it to me on New Year's Day; I asked for it,

I want it, and now I order it under holy obedience. Sr. A. Angela, be sensible; don't be careless, so that I can understand it properly.4

3. Sr. A. Vincenza is now writing to Squarzoni. For the moment it is really impossible for me to come; there are too many things, and the forthcoming clothing of this young lady weighs heavily on me and keeps me very busy.2

4. My dear, don't think you are far from me, no, for perhaps you are closer to me than if I had you at my side. Not a minute passes without my thoughts being with you and in your actions; I always try, in God's presence, to be close to you.

5. You see, my beloved daughter, it is good that I settle things here now, because when it is done I shall have to come there and stay a good while. Come, think about it and you will see that this is what the Lord's work requires.

6. My health: for two days I have been on my feet without lying down, and certain fainting fits that worried me a good deal, for fear one might catch me,3 have stopped.

7. Take care of yourself and be cheerful.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me always your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

God bless all the others; please greet them for me, together with the little girls.

Once again I am your

Affectionate MOTHER R. P.S. Have them pray hard for the Countess, for charity's sake.

She can offer hospitality in the poor house, so that they can be with their daughter as they wish.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

1. As you left without my knowing, before I could offer you anything, not even our wretched lodging, I was very sorry.

2. Since the people we were expecting from Genoa today did not arrive, if Your Ladyship would honour us with your presence, Mother and daughter could occupy it night and day, and the father, the Marquis, only a few hours a day.1

3. With all my heart I will offer you what we have, so that you can be with your daughter2 as you wish.

With every esteem and respect I remain Your Ladyship's

most humble Sr. A. M. ROSA G.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc55: Courage... after her pointed reminder that trial is needed for full human and Christian growth, the Mother adds, as a further invitation to accept and live courageously the hardships of poverty, the teaching of the «three richest personages of heaven». notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc232: Would have done better... said evidently in jest, alluding to the difficulties she met in God's Work.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc235: She has no joyful news to tell, only sad news.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc236: Sorrow upon sorrow... Golgotha? She does not speak to him of the painful side of daily life but of the crucifying effect it has on her, and with spontaneous trust invites him to dwell with her, in a fellowship of friendship, on Golgotha, to rejoice in the Redeemer's suffering.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc237: On 1 October the liturgical feast of Our Lady of the Rosary was celebrated.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc238: Dear Mary had granted her the grace of spending the whole day sweetly clinging to the feet of Jesus, immersed in his wounds; otherwise she could not have withstood the thrusts of every kind.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc239: To please the dear Eternal Father: the supreme aspiration of her life.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc240: What a little madcap: she uses this expression to tone down the force of her mystical ardour. He... console them. This passage seems difficult to interpret.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc243: Dear... dear... dear; I will always be with you. Sr. A. Vincenza was extremely delicate and sensitive. The Mother, generally «brisk», knows how to adapt to the needs of this dear daughter, who is maturing in «pure love».
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc244: After Sr. A. Adelaide left for Ferrara, the acting Superior was Sr. A. Concetta Vernengo. Cf. L 131, 3.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc245: His Excellency Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli; Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist, his secretary.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc246: It was necessary not only to choose and furnish suitable rooms but also to carry out building work to adapt the whole property.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc249: Whether they reach you, are delivered to you.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc253: We have not been called to nurse the sick at home.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc254: The Cardinal Protector: Luigi Vannicelli, mentioned above.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc256: The two graces are stated below, in par. 2.

The Work, which already included the school and home nursing, was thus becoming more complex.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc259: The Mother invites her to accept in obedience a choice weighed before God; she herself had followed the will of the Superiors (Fr Tornatore and the Church authority).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc260: Nothing good... She means no joy deriving from human satisfactions, only the pure joy that comes from acting solely for the Lord.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc261: By the Superior of the Ferrara community, Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc263: Father, perhaps Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist, whom she also called Father.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc264: Sr. A. Clementina Reggi died on 11 October 1871.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc265: Mother Rosa had a sense of the preciousness of time, linked to diligent industry moved by love of God and neighbour.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc266: Before the feast of All Saints. She did in fact return on 30 October, as L 123 shows.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc267: Certainly after the liturgical commemoration of the dead, that is, on 3 November; a building job all still to be done: cf. L 108, n. 5.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc268: Beneath my pains = though subject to my usual pains.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc270: The date follows from the context and, through the detail given in paragraph 4, from the 1871 calendar.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc271: The sad news. Father Agostino had written to her on 13 October 1871: «...yesterday I visited Mgr Vitelleschi, the new Secretary (of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars), and we spoke at length about the Rule... and he told me that with that Rule you will never see your Institute approved, and that in his opinion it should be withdrawn from all the houses, and that I should write and tell you so, my good mother...». The news seemed incredible to her: And yet it will be that Rule, and then everyone will be convinced. Her certainty of the «goodness» of that Rule sustained her through the uncertain and tormented process of its approval.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc273: Prompt obedience: before instilling it in her daughters she practised it herself: «I will lose no time in flying».
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc274: Countess Maria Anna Trotti left on Thursday the 22nd.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc275: Said in jest: Carlotta and Sr. A. Adelaide, who, seeing her alone at last, joke to keep her cheerful.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc278: Cf. L 111, 5 and 8. After Sr. A. Clementina Reggi, whose death she had reported, Sr. A. Luigia Mussi had also died, on 16 October.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc279: Noticing the Mother's silence, Sr. A. Francesca grieved, imagining a thousand things and believing herself forgotten as unworthy.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc280: The Mother helps her understand the quality and depth of her maternal love and the plans she cherishes for her, entrusting her to Saint Anne and the Eternal Father.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc281: Rest assured... with you. Words full of human understanding, reassuring and affectionate: I will soon be with you.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc282: Alessandro (she still called him by the pet name Gigino) was unhappy with the environment at Mondovì, as his letters to his mother show. Fr Tornatore had made enquiries about a possible place at the «S. Giorgio» boarding college in Novi Ligure. On her way to Genoa she passed through Novi Ligure station.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc283: The painful scene... the debts. A truly painful reality, the debts, never entirely paid off.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc284: Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli, Archbishop of Ferrara, had been Protector of the Institute since 4 June 1871.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc290: I took... our soul. She immerses her with herself, through the wound in the Side, in the Heart of Jesus, that he may consume her, uniting her intimately to himself and transforming her so that her body is no longer subject to the senses of the flesh but is only an instrument of sanctification. Cf. St Paul, Rom 8:11-13.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc291: Loving cave: the seat and source of love.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc292: In the Heart of Jesus we find every consolation; every pain vanishes and one tastes only true and perfect joy; so the ardent desire, the hunger for suffering arises in the soul, because the more we are weighed down by pain, the more Jesus lets us penetrate the most hidden secrets of his Side (= the heart pierced by the lance), where the beatitude of paradise is enjoyed in advance. This is Mother Rosa's very personal experience of the beatitude (cf. Mt 5:4): blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc293: Only one... happiness. The only difference between earthly and heavenly joy is this: what we feel now is only a foretaste of the other and is always accompanied by bitterness (the bitter cup); but it is precisely the cup that pours into our soul the purest essence of God's love. This then is our Paradise, our immense consolations: joy united with pains, for it is precisely these that are the pledge of eternal happiness.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc294: The logical consequence is to turn to the Father, asking him with filial trust to look on her and give her his life-giving strength to carry the cross clasped to her breast and finally rest on it, handing over her life to the Bridegroom.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc295: She ends with an intense invocation of suffering: delight, pledge that unites her with an indissoluble bond to the Most Holy Trinity. Having closed her spiritual teaching with Amen, she turns simply and with warm human attention to the small things of daily life.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc296: Final recommendations: to give a note to Sr. A. Concetta Vernengo; greetings and a request for prayers for the Cardinal Protector Luigi Vannicelli; for Countess Trotti she asks more intense prayer, as she has a lawsuit in progress with her husband's relatives; Carolina too should pray (probably the postulant C. Viani, who entered in June of that year).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc297: She takes on the suffering of her daughter Francesca and shares her anguish. Our tears are legitimate. Jesus wept for Lazarus; Mary wept doubly for her son, torn in his humanity and dead. Our grief, even if it breaks our heart, must root us in love, peace and acceptance of God's will.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc298: The preceding reflections lead into this «golden maxim» of spiritual wisdom, dear to the Saints, and open the central teaching of the letter: the value of suffering, a theme to which Mother Rosa returned insistently: this blessed Mother can talk of nothing but suffering.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc299: This explains why she dwells on this pleasant subject: in «suffering», which drives her to plunge into the Side of Jesus, she finds sweetness, love and peace.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc300: But... take note: the soul cannot reach the unitive experience except after the purification of suffering.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc301: She asked the Eternal Father for this grace for her daughter. Jesus told her that the simple sweets, that is, small pains with their accompanying inner consolations, he reserves for little, childlike souls; great burdens of suffering he reserves for souls he wants beautiful, great and strong.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc302: Moving naturally from the spiritual to the temporal, she approves the requests: it is good to whitewash the rooms, paint the beds, wash the sheets, etc.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc303: Father Agostino had replied on 18 October to her letter of the 16th (cf. L 113) with a «curt and melancholy» letter. He apologises for saddening her about the Rule, but he had written only what Fr Angelini had told him, and the advice to come to Rome was also that Father's. The letter does indeed match Mother Rosa's description.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc304: The letter of 8 October had not been delivered to her. She had good reason to fear interference by an enemy: that monster of a P., Don Luigi Cogrossi, was in Piacenza. After she had removed him from the Institute in August 1867 (cf. Lettere 1, p. 528), he continued to oppose it. She jokingly calls him Cepinetto (her name for the devil) because of his harmful actions.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc305: Since I have not received the letter (of 8 October), I am unable to reply to Fr Angelini...
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc306: She continues to teach her Vincenza and help her sublimate the affection that draws her to her spiritual Mother. Every teaching device serves. This time she brings in the Sacred Heart, speaking to her with persuasive and gentle words.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc307: She refers to the Sister's attachment to her, so strong that she suffered greatly when the Mother was away.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc308: Fragrant rose, that «surpasses all spices», like the bride of the Song. Cf. Song 4:10.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc309: Date deduced from the context and particularly from L 118.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc310: The Delegate of the House in Via della Morte was Sr. A. Francesca Camisa.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc311: Sig. Giuseppe Brigidini, friend and benefactor of the Institute, was selling tickets for a lottery whose proceeds would help reduce, if only slightly, the community's deficit.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc313: The black bodice — the bodice of the habit... was dear to me. This expression is very well known among the Daughters of Saint Anne because it sharply conveys the Mother's great love for and observance of poverty.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc314: What she meant to ask cannot be deduced.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc315: The whole day: probably Sunday the 29th, since she was to confer with Countess Maria Anna Trotti; or only part of the 30th.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc316: She had hoped to finish earlier in order to visit Gigino (her son Alessandro) at the College in Novi Ligure.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc318: It is known that she suffered greatly when travelling. Her emotion springs from gratitude to her daughters and a spontaneous movement of love towards the Father, who heard their prayers.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc319: The addition is for Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, Superior of the new community. She advises her to place a Sister alongside the lay teacher.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc320: She had not given her enough shawls to keep warm during the journey.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc321: Don Gaetano Bersani, a priest and friend of Alessandro, was in all likelihood taking him to the College in Novi Ligure.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc322: This was the usual way of referring to the House located there.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc323: It is the trusting prayer of a mother who entrusts her daughter to the Father so that she may act well for the good of the Work, and asks him to keep this daughter of hers who is his gift: it was you who gave her to me.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc326: For fear the letters may go astray, she addresses them to the House in Genoa, Via del Castelletto.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc328: This is certainly the date. She had asked Sr. A. Vincenza to go to Sampierdarena to visit the community.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc330: Signora Caterina Rusca. Cf. L 36, n. 7; 94, n. 3.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc331: or, failing that, if this were lacking or not possible.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc333: Back in Piacenza after almost a month's absence, she had several problems to settle urgently before leaving again.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc348: Monsignor: the Bishop of Ferrara, Luigi Giordani; Giuseppe Squarzoni, Countess Maria Anna Trotti's steward.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc349: The Sister is referring to L 130, 4. The Parish Priest: Don Gaetano Ferri.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc352: Perhaps: succeeds in obtaining the increase in Sisters we want.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc509: with the savings. She means: at no cost to the «Charity Board», since with the L. 400 stipend the community, by its own savings, could support an extra Sister or two, given the great need for home nursing.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc511: This date is presumed, bearing in mind that the young woman was to receive the religious habit on 10 February. Cf. L 164, 2.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc512: The Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Antonio Ranza.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc513: Fr Giuseppe Manfredini was a friend of the Countess. The Mother had asked him to support the vocational choice of the Marchioness Maria Maddalena Durazzo. Cf. L 161.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc514: It is not known who the housekeeper was, nor what problem she was causing.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc515: The count she mentions is Mgr Domenico Tellarini, cousin of Countess Trotti.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc516: The benches for the School. She hopes the Charity Board will provide them and the School can soon open.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc517: the attendant: the servant who had been hired. Cf. L 162, n. 1.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc518: Having no acute illness. The Agreement between the "Charity Board" and the "Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne", signed on 12 January 1872, provided for admission to the Hospital of "patients with acute illness". The Mother is keen to clarify the observance of this point of the Agreement and the exception to it, should Count Galvagno, as President of the Charity Board, accept in a personal capacity a patient not in the acute phase.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc519: The experienced Sister was Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni, who had done good training and gained experience in the Hospital at Cento.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc520: The letter referred to is of 10 February '72.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc521:
The Parish Priest had asked her, among other things: "When the Countess stops supporting you, will she leave you some endowment?". The Sister had replied that she knew nothing about it and had added: "We trust in God and in his providence".

And the Parish Priest: "We'll think about it; we'll approach some pious person...". The Mother praises her daughter for her words.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc522: The Countess will one day say: I'm stopping helping the Sisters. Cf. L 179, n. 3.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc523: She suggests other people to approach: Parish Priest Gaetano Ferri, Don Ignazio, Mgr Antonelli.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc524: She should, however, use discretion, taking account of health.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc525: But she must not stop there: she must enquire and ask anyone who, though suffering, might not want to say anything, how she feels and whether she can do her work as usual.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc526: She had asked her for the accounts summary, with income and expenditure for the whole year. As it had not been sent, she orders it under obedience and, addressing directly the one compiling it, Sr. A. Angiola Degrossi, tells her not to be careless (sbadattarti) so that the summary is clear.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc527: The two Sisters, Sr. A. Giustina Mazzocchi and Sr. A. Elena Ferrari, had not been given their personal trousseau. This had happened before. For four Sisters she had had to provide trousseau linen again.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc528: She will ask (incombenserò) the Delegate in Genoa, Sr. A. Serafina Lorenzi, to obtain straw mattresses.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc529: As for the other Sisters lacking personal linen, she must first send her the inventory of their trousseau.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc531: Through the Sister, Sr. A. Concetta Vernengo.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc532: During Lent brown bread, but in sufficient quantity; and each should eat according to her need.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc534:
The steward Giuseppe Squarzoni had visited the house and told her of the need to confer with the Mother to decide various matters. She will have Sr. A. Vincenza write to him. It is impossible to leave Piacenza; among other things, the clothing of the Marchioness M. Maddalena Durazzo is imminent. Cf. L 161;

163; 164; 169.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc536: She was very sorry because, as they left without her knowing, she had not been able to offer anything or even put them up. She offers overnight hospitality to her and her daughter Giovanna.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnc537:
With her daughter Maria Maddalena, a postulant there.

notes.lettere-en-v2-fnx43801: Cav. Dr Pietro Matteucci, a friend of the Countess and of Fr Manfredini.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny1: The date too is deduced from the latter.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny2: The date follows from some expressions in the text that recur in other letters of this period. Cf. par. 7 and 9; also L 70, n. 7; 72, n. 5; 75, 3.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny3: She takes her painful physical illness as an occasion to teach the sublime science of suffering for and with Jesus. Only with him does suffering turn positive: cross-love.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny4: The Marchioness Teresa Cambiaso, her friend. Three letters and a postcard from her, written between 1865 and 1883, survive.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny5: Don Luigi Decavi had presented four postulants. Paola Liberti, Sr. A. Cherubina, had been clothed on 21 August 1871; for the others 17 September had been chosen, eight days after the feast of Mary's Nativity.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny6: Patience, courage: the strong virtues for the hard road of following Jesus; prudence: the light that always chooses what «leads to acquiring and increasing the only wealth, namely the love of God» (Rule of '69, p. 25).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny8: The postulant must on no account nurse the sick.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny9: A stern warning to all the nurses: if they are negligent in their duty, the Superiors will have to intervene severely.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fny10: Sr. A. Ignazia Losi (the Sister who negligently fell asleep) needs a special admonition. She must also know that the Mother had constantly felt great sorrow for the Ferrara house because of her failing (dreadful damage), which could have brought discredit on the whole religious Family.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw1: The date follows from a letter of Fr Tornatore of 13 June 1871 to the Superior Paola Bucciotti about Sr. A. Ernesta's faults and how to deal with her. Since M. Rosa says below, «Tomorrow I will speak to the Father about it and I hope he will write himself», this letter is evidently of 12 June.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw2: Cf. previous L (69) 1-2 and the relevant notes.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw3: They are let pass, such faults are tolerated; it cannot be avoided that they suffer from the bad example.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw4: Once one fault has been corrected and amended, you will take up another, and the evil will be removed.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw5: The Father, informed, wrote the same day: 13 June 1871 (cf. AFSA, 1).
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw7: That she may finish soon. Everything is getting complicated. The Holy Father had had the Rule and other documents sent to the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, the Dicastery competent for examination and judgement. The matter therefore could not be settled at once. Cf. L 65, n. 3.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw8: Fr Tornatore's letter bears the same date: 4 August 1871. The unfortunate creature is Sr. A. Addolorata Gianni, who in the Sampierdarena community had repeatedly been disrespectful to her Superior, to the grave scandal of the Sisters. She has now been moved to the Genoa community on trial, but must do penance: go to Sampierdarena and ask the community's forgiveness.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw10: Presumably a benefactor who undertook in writing to give a monthly offering to the house. Cf. L 90, 4.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw12: Writing to Sr. A. Serafina Lorenzi, she had forgotten the usual opening invocations: «The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us» and «Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate». She is not to be scandalised or take a bad example from her.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw13: The Sisters had arrived in Ferrara a few days earlier, on the 4th; cf. letter of 8 October from Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, Superior of the new community, to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino (AFSA, F 3, 28). Significantly, the work began with the blessing of the Chapel.
notes.lettere-en-v2-fnw14: Adapting the large and stately Palazzo Obizzi to its new use — a house for the Sisters, a boarding house and school for girls — was certainly neither easy nor simple.
